samples.stem: Prions are infectious particles composed of
samples.why: Prions are acellular infectious particles made of protein only, with no nucleic acid at all. They are not considered living organisms. Viroids, by contrast, are made of circular RNA only.

wrong.0: Particles made of circular RNA only are viroids, not prions.
wrong.1: Nucleic acid such as DNA surrounded by a protein coat describes a virus.
wrong.3: RNA with a lipid envelope describes an enveloped RNA virus such as influenza virus.

samples.stem: The guidelines for classifying viruses are set by the
options: International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV)
International Union for Conservation of Nature
samples.why: Viruses are classified by their genetic material, replication strategy, shape and host range. The guidelines for this classification are set by the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV).

wrong.1: The World Health Organization deals with global public health. It does not set the rules for virus classification.
wrong.2: The IUCN works on nature conservation and threatened species, not virus taxonomy.
wrong.3: The PMDC is Pakistan's medical and dental regulatory body. It has no role in classifying viruses.

samples.stem: Sulfolobus spindle-shaped virus is an example of a virus that infects
samples.why: By host range, viruses are grouped as animal viruses, plant viruses, bacteriophages and archaea viruses. Sulfolobus spindle-shaped virus infects Sulfolobus, an archaeon, so it is an archaea virus.

wrong.0: Viruses that infect bacteria are bacteriophages, such as T4 phage and lambda phage.
wrong.1: Plant viruses include tobacco mosaic virus and potato virus X.
wrong.2: Animal viruses include influenza virus and rabies virus.

samples.stem: Fritz Lipmann's contribution in 1941 was to propose that ATP
options: is the main energy-transfer molecule in the cell
samples.why: Karl Lohmann discovered ATP in 1929. In 1941 Fritz Lipmann proposed that ATP is the main energy-transfer molecule in the cell. Cells make ATP when they release energy from food and break it when they need energy, so it links the two kinds of reactions.

wrong.0: ATP is made in both mitochondria and chloroplasts, and in the cytoplasm too. Lipmann's idea concerned its role, not its site.
wrong.1: ATP contains ribose, not deoxyribose. Deoxyribose is the sugar of DNA.
wrong.2: Genetic information is stored in DNA. ATP is an energy carrier.

samples.stem: Oxidation of one NADH in the electron transport chain produces
samples.why: When NADH passes its electrons into the chain, enough H⁺ is pumped to make three ATP by chemiosmosis. FADH₂ enters later, at coenzyme Q, so its oxidation yields only two ATP.

wrong.0: One ATP is too low. Each NADH oxidised in the chain gives three ATP.
wrong.1: Two ATP come from each FADH₂ (and from each NADH of glycolysis after transport costs), not from an ordinary NADH.
wrong.3: Four ATP is too high. The figure for one NADH is three.

samples.stem: The three subunits of an ATP molecule are
options: adenine, deoxyribose and three phosphate groups
adenosine, glucose and two phosphate groups
adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups
guanine, ribose and three phosphate groups
samples.why: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is a nucleotide with three subunits. Adenine is the nitrogen-containing base, ribose is the five-carbon sugar, and three phosphate groups are attached in a row. The bonds between the phosphates are the high-energy bonds.

wrong.0: Deoxyribose is the sugar of DNA nucleotides. The sugar in ATP is ribose.
wrong.1: Glucose is not part of ATP, and ATP has three phosphates, not two. Adenosine with two phosphates is ADP.
wrong.3: Guanine with ribose and three phosphates makes GTP. The base in ATP is adenine.

samples.stem: Sweating and transpiration cool organisms because water has a
samples.why: Water has a high heat of vaporisation, so it absorbs a lot of heat when it changes from liquid to vapour. As sweat or transpired water evaporates, each gram removes about 574 calories of heat from the body surface, cooling the organism.

wrong.0: Water has a high specific heat, not a low one, and specific heat is not what cools by evaporation.
wrong.1: Maximum density at 4 °C explains why ice floats. It has nothing to do with sweating.
wrong.3: Water has high cohesion, and cohesion explains water transport in xylem, not cooling.

samples.stem: A protein made of two or more polypeptide chains, each with tertiary structure, held together has
samples.why: Quaternary structure is formed when two or more polypeptide chains, each already folded into a tertiary structure, are held together. Hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds and ionic bonds keep the chains joined. Haemoglobin, with two alpha and two beta chains, is an example.

wrong.0: Primary structure is only the sequence of amino acids in a chain. It says nothing about how separate chains are combined.
wrong.1: Secondary structure is the coiling (alpha helix) or folding (pleated sheet) within one chain, held by hydrogen bonds.
wrong.2: Tertiary structure is the globular folding of a single chain. Joining several folded chains goes one level further, to quaternary.

samples.stem: Which of these is a globular protein?
samples.why: Globular proteins are folded into a compact, roughly spherical shape, are soluble and do functional work such as transport or catalysis. Haemoglobin is a globular protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells. Keratin, collagen and fibrin are long fibrous proteins with structural roles.

wrong.0: Keratin is a fibrous structural protein found in hair, nails, horns and the outer layer of skin.
wrong.1: Collagen is a fibrous structural protein that gives strength to tendons, bone, cartilage and skin.
wrong.2: Fibrin is a fibrous protein that forms the mesh of threads in a blood clot.

samples.stem: Primers used in PCR are about
samples.why: A primer is a short single-stranded piece of nucleic acid that binds to the DNA template and gives the polymerase a starting point. In PCR an excess of primers about 20 to 30 nucleotides long is mixed with the DNA. This length is long enough to bind only at the target site.

wrong.0: Primers of 2 to 3 nucleotides would match many places in the DNA, so they could not bind specifically.
wrong.2: 200 to 300 nucleotides is much longer than PCR primers, which are about 20 to 30 nucleotides.
wrong.3: 2000 to 3000 nucleotides is far too long for a primer; that is the size of a whole gene fragment.

samples.stem: Pectin-esterase produced by transgenic bacteria is used to
options: clot milk protein for cheese making
improve the clarity of fruit juice
samples.why: Transgenic bacteria are also used to make enzymes for the food industry. Pectin-esterase acts on pectin, which makes fruit juice cloudy, and so improves the clarity of fruit juice.

wrong.0: Dissolving blood clots is the job of tissue plasminogen activator, another product of transgenic bacteria.
wrong.1: Clotting milk protein for cheese making is done by chymosin.
wrong.2: Converting starch into simple sugars is done by alpha-amylase.

samples.stem: Traditional biotechnology, used for thousands of years to make bread, cheese and beer, is based on
samples.why: Traditional biotechnology has been used for thousands of years through fermentation. Microorganisms such as yeast and bacteria change food materials, giving bread, cheese and beer. Modern biotechnology began in the 20th century after the structure of DNA was discovered.

wrong.0: Recombinant DNA technology is modern biotechnology, which began in the 20th century.
wrong.1: PCR is a modern technique, developed by Kary Mullis in 1983.
wrong.3: Gene guns are a modern method for shooting DNA into plant cells. They were not used in ancient food making.

samples.stem: The bacterial chromosome in the nucleoid is
options: several linear DNA molecules wrapped on histones
a single circular double-stranded DNA without histones
samples.why: A bacterium has a single, circular, double-stranded DNA molecule lying in an irregular dense region of the cytoplasm called the nucleoid. This DNA has no histones attached and no nuclear membrane around it, and is sometimes called the bacterial chromosome.

wrong.0: Several linear DNA molecules wrapped on histones describe eukaryotic chromosomes.
wrong.1: The genetic material of bacteria is double-stranded DNA, not single-stranded RNA.
wrong.3: Bacteria are prokaryotes. Their nucleoid has no nuclear membrane around it.

samples.stem: In a mitochondrion, the enzymes of the Krebs cycle are found in the
samples.why: The matrix is the large internal space beneath the inner membrane of a mitochondrion. Enzymes in the matrix catalyse some steps of respiration, such as the Krebs cycle, while the electron transport proteins sit on the inner membrane.

wrong.0: The outer membrane is smooth and acts like a sieve, filtering out molecules that are too big.
wrong.1: The intermembrane space is the narrow gap between the two membranes, not where the Krebs cycle runs.
wrong.3: F-1 particles are ATP synthase enzymes on the cristae, not Krebs cycle enzymes.

samples.stem: In the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane, the word "fluid" refers to the fact that
options: the membrane is made of water
phospholipids and many proteins can move sideways within the bilayer
the membrane has no fixed thickness
proteins are dissolved in the cytoplasm
samples.why: The fluid mosaic model, proposed by Singer and Nicolson in 1972, describes the membrane as a phospholipid bilayer with proteins scattered through it. Fluid means the lipids and many proteins can move sideways within the bilayer, like a two-dimensional liquid. Mosaic refers to the pattern of proteins.

wrong.0: The membrane is made of lipids and proteins, not of water.
wrong.2: Membrane thickness is fairly constant, about 7 to 10 nm. Fluid refers to movement of molecules, not changing thickness.
wrong.3: Membrane proteins are embedded in or attached to the bilayer, not dissolved in the cytoplasm.

samples.stem: In the Hershey–Chase experiment, the protein coats of bacteriophages were labelled with
samples.why: Hershey and Chase used isotopes that label only one kind of molecule. Sulphur is found in some amino acids of proteins but not in DNA, so ³⁵S labelled the protein coats. Phosphorus is found in DNA phosphate groups but not in protein, so ³²P labelled the DNA.

wrong.1: ³²P was used to label the DNA, because phosphorus is in the phosphate groups of DNA and not in proteins.
wrong.2: ¹⁵N, a heavy isotope, was used by Meselson and Stahl to study DNA replication.
wrong.3: ¹⁴C is present in both DNA and protein, so it could not tell them apart and was not used.

samples.stem: Eukaryotic mRNA becomes shorter before translation mainly because
options: introns are removed by splicing and the exons are joined
exons are removed and introns joined
samples.why: Newly made eukaryotic mRNA is immature because it contains introns, non-coding regions, between the exons. Splicing cuts out the introns and joins the exons. So the mature mRNA is shorter and carries only coding sequences.

wrong.1: The 5′ cap is added, not removed, and it does not shorten the mRNA.
wrong.2: This reverses splicing. Exons are kept and joined; introns are removed.
wrong.3: A poly-A tail is added at the 3′ end, which makes the mRNA longer. It is not doubled.

samples.stem: The DNA in an average human chromosome is about
options: 5 cm long, with about 140 million nucleotides
samples.why: Each chromosome holds one very long DNA molecule packed tightly with histone proteins. In an average human chromosome this DNA is about 5 cm long and contains about 140 million nucleotides. Packing by histones lets it fit into a nucleus only a few micrometres wide.

wrong.0: 2 nm is the width of the DNA double helix, and 146 nucleotides is the DNA wrapped around one nucleosome.
wrong.1: 700 nm is the thickness of a fully condensed chromatid, not the length of its DNA.
wrong.3: About 20,000 is the number of human genes in total, not the nucleotides in one chromosome, and 1 m is not its length.

samples.stem: In sickle cell anaemia, the DNA codon change that replaces glutamic acid with valine is
options: CTC → CAC, a substitution of T by A
samples.why: Sickle cell anaemia comes from a single point mutation in the β-globin gene. The DNA base T is replaced by A, so the codon CTC, which codes glutamic acid, becomes CAC, which codes valine. Changing one amino acid this way makes it a missense mutation.

wrong.1: GGC → GGU still codes glycine, so it is a silent mutation and does not change the protein.
wrong.2: Transposon insertion into the factor IX gene is an example of insertional inactivation causing haemophilia.
wrong.3: Deletion of three nucleotides is the common cause of cystic fibrosis, not sickle cell anaemia.

samples.stem: Neurons that lie entirely within the CNS and link sensory neurons to motor neurons are
samples.why: Inter-neurons, also called associative neurons, lie entirely within the brain and spinal cord. They receive impulses from sensory neurons or other inter-neurons and pass them on to motor neurons or other inter-neurons, so they process information.

wrong.0: Motor neurons have their cell bodies in the CNS, but their axons extend out of it to reach effectors.
wrong.1: Sensory neurons bring impulses from receptors into the CNS. Their cell bodies lie outside it in ganglia.
wrong.2: Schwann cells are glial cells of the peripheral nervous system that make myelin. They are not neurons.

samples.stem: The average adult human brain weighs about
samples.why: The average adult human brain weighs about 1.4 kg, roughly 2% of total body weight. Even so, it contains about 100 billion inter-neurons, each of which forms synapses with several thousand other neurons.

wrong.1: 4 kg is almost three times too heavy. An adult brain weighs about 1.4 kg, about 2% of body weight.
wrong.2: 0.4 kg is far too light for an adult brain. The true figure is about 1.4 kg.
wrong.3: 14 kg is ten times too heavy and would be about a fifth of the whole body.

samples.stem: Drug tolerance means that
options: the person can stop the drug without any symptoms
the drug becomes more effective with each dose
the drug is no longer psychoactive
the body becomes less sensitive to the drug, so higher doses are needed for the same effect
samples.why: With continued use of a drug, the body adapts and becomes less sensitive to it. This is drug tolerance. The person then needs higher doses to get the same effect as before, which tends to deepen addiction.

wrong.0: Stopping a drug after dependence usually causes withdrawal symptoms such as headache, insomnia and anxiety.
wrong.1: Tolerance is the opposite. Each dose gives a smaller effect, so the drug seems less effective over time.
wrong.2: The drug still acts on the brain. The brain has simply become less responsive to the same dose.

samples.stem: FSH and LH are together called
samples.why: FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) and LH (luteinizing hormone) both act on the gonads, the testes and ovaries. For this reason they are together called gonadotropins. Both are glycoprotein hormones made by the anterior pituitary.

wrong.0: Corticosteroids, such as cortisol and aldosterone, are steroid hormones of the adrenal cortex.
wrong.2: Catecholamines are hormones such as epinephrine from the adrenal medulla, not FSH and LH.
wrong.3: FSH and LH are made by the anterior pituitary, not by the neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus.

samples.stem: The thymus gland secretes thymosin, which
options: stimulates the maturation of T cells
samples.why: The thymus gland lies beneath the sternum, between the lungs. It secretes the hormone thymosin, which stimulates the maturation of T cells. T cells are white blood cells that help defend the body against pathogens.

wrong.0: Sleep patterns are regulated by melatonin from the pineal gland.
wrong.2: Bile release from the gallbladder is stimulated by cholecystokinin from the small intestine wall.
wrong.3: Blood calcium is raised by parathormone from the parathyroid glands.

samples.stem: Pepsin is produced in the inactive form pepsinogen because
options: active pepsin could digest protein structures inside the cell that makes it
pepsin cannot be made by ribosomes
samples.why: Pepsin is a protein-digesting enzyme. If it were active inside the cell that makes it, it could digest that cell's own protein structures. So it is made and secreted as inactive pepsinogen, and it is activated to pepsin only when it reaches its site of action in the stomach.

wrong.1: Pepsin, like all enzymes, is made on ribosomes. Being made in an inactive form protects the cell, not the ribosome.
wrong.2: Pepsinogen is the inactive form of a protease. It does not digest fats.
wrong.3: Pepsinogen is in fact activated in the stomach, which is its target site. That is the whole point of secreting it inactive.

samples.stem: Inhibitors of enzymes involved in blood clotting are used as
samples.why: Enzyme inhibitors are used to manage many medical conditions. Blood clotting depends on a chain of enzymes. Drugs that inhibit some of these enzymes slow clot formation, so they are used as anticoagulants (anti-clotting drugs).

wrong.0: Antibiotics inhibit enzymes needed by bacteria, such as the cell wall enzyme blocked by penicillin, not clotting enzymes.
wrong.1: Biopesticides are living organisms or their products used to control pests, not clotting inhibitors.
wrong.3: Coenzymes help enzymes to work. They are not inhibitors of clotting enzymes.

samples.stem: Enzymes speed up chemical reactions by
options: being used up in the reaction
samples.why: Every reaction needs some activation energy to break existing bonds and get started. Enzymes, the biocatalysts of the cell, lower this activation energy, so the reaction runs much faster. The enzyme itself comes out of the reaction unchanged and can be used again.

wrong.0: Raising the activation energy would slow a reaction down. Enzymes do the opposite and lower it.
wrong.1: Enzymes do not change what is made. Sucrose gives glucose and fructose with or without sucrase.
wrong.2: Enzymes are not used up. They leave the reaction unaltered and can catalyse it again and again.

samples.stem: In Darwin's theory, variations that help individuals survive and reproduce are called
samples.why: Because more offspring are produced than resources can support, individuals struggle to survive. Those with helpful variations survive and reproduce more successfully. Darwin called such helpful variations adaptive traits, and they are passed to the next generation.

wrong.0: Acquired characters are changes gained by use or disuse during life, in Lamarck's theory.
wrong.2: Vestigial structures are remnants that have lost their use, such as the human appendix.
wrong.3: Analogous organs have the same function but different structure, such as bird and insect wings.

samples.stem: According to Darwin's thinking on the finches, a new species arises when
options: an individual stretches its organs during its lifetime
it is created in a new habitat in its present form
a population separated from the original habitat gradually accumulates adaptations to a different environment
two species merge into one by interbreeding
samples.why: Darwin linked the origin of new species with adaptation. When a population is separated from its original habitat, it gradually accumulates adaptations to its new environment. Over many generations the two populations become so different that they are separate species, as with the Galápagos finches.

wrong.0: Stretching organs during life and passing the change on is Lamarck's idea of use and disuse.
wrong.1: Creation in a new habitat in present form is creationism, not Darwin's explanation.
wrong.3: Darwin described populations dividing and diverging into new species, not two species merging into one.

samples.stem: The view that every type of organism was created individually in its present form and has not changed is called
samples.why: Creationism, also called the theory of intelligent design, holds that all organisms were created as they exist today. Creationists claim each type of organism was created individually and has not changed through history. This is the opposite of evolution.

wrong.0: Spontaneous generation is the old idea that living things can arise from non-living matter.
wrong.1: Lamarckism is a theory of evolution, so it accepts that organisms change over time.
wrong.2: Neo-Darwinism combines Darwin's natural selection with genetics. It describes change, not fixed forms.

samples.stem: Which three elements work together to maintain homeostasis?
samples.why: Homeostasis depends on three elements working as a loop. Receptors detect a change, the control centre processes the information and decides on a response, and effectors carry out that response to bring the body back to its set point.

wrong.0: Neurons and hormones are ways of carrying messages between parts of the loop. They are not the three named elements of homeostasis.
wrong.1: Enzymes and blood are not parts of the homeostatic loop. Only the control centre in this list is one of the three elements.
wrong.3: Kidneys and skin are organs that can act as effectors in some responses, but they are not the three basic elements of homeostasis.

samples.stem: Ectotherms depend on heat from their environment mainly because
options: their metabolic rate is too low to produce enough body heat
they have thick insulation of fat and feathers
they cannot move to new places
samples.why: Ectotherms such as fishes, amphibians and reptiles have a very low metabolic rate. They cannot produce enough internal heat to raise and keep a steady body temperature, so they depend on heat from the environment and use behaviour, such as basking, to control it.

wrong.1: Fishes, amphibians and reptiles do have a hypothalamus. Their dependence on outside heat comes from their low metabolic rate.
wrong.2: Insulation by fat, hair or feathers is a feature of endotherms. It helps keep internally produced heat in the body.
wrong.3: Ectotherms can move. They move into the sun, onto warm rocks or into shade as a way of controlling their temperature.

samples.stem: A normal adult passes about 1–2 L of urine a day. Which change would decrease urine volume?
options: Eating a diet high in salt
samples.why: Urine volume depends on how much water the body needs to keep. A diet high in salt raises the salt concentration of the blood, so the body retains water to dilute it. More water is reabsorbed and urine output falls.

wrong.0: Drinking more fluids adds extra water to the body, so the kidneys pass more urine, not less.
wrong.1: Low ADH makes collecting ducts less permeable, so less water is reabsorbed and urine volume increases.
wrong.3: In cool weather little water is lost as sweat, so the kidneys do not need to conserve water and urine volume rises.

samples.stem: Very low temperatures affect the lipid bilayer of cell membranes by making it
samples.why: Cell membranes are built from a lipid bilayer whose properties depend on temperature. Very low temperatures make the membrane rigid and brittle, while high temperatures can make it lose its selective permeability.

wrong.0: Permanent denaturation describes enzymes at high temperatures, not membranes in the cold.
wrong.1: Cold does not make membranes better at controlling what passes. It makes them stiff and brittle.
wrong.3: Losing selective permeability is the effect of high temperatures, not low ones.

samples.stem: The antibiotic penicillin is removed from the blood by the kidneys much faster than glomerular filtration alone could achieve. This is because penicillin is
options: reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule
filtered only, at a higher pressure than other solutes
broken down in the loop of Henle
actively secreted from the peritubular capillaries into the tubule
samples.why: Tubular secretion actively moves certain substances from the blood in the peritubular capillaries into the tubule. Examples are H⁺, K⁺ and drugs such as penicillin. This adds to the amount already filtered at the glomerulus, so penicillin is removed faster than by filtration alone.

wrong.0: Reabsorption returns a substance to the blood, which would slow its removal, not speed it up.
wrong.1: All small solutes are filtered at the same glomerular pressure. There is no special higher pressure for penicillin.
wrong.2: The loop of Henle helps concentrate urine. It does not break down drugs.

samples.stem: The sight, smell or thought of food causes a small secretion of gastric juice through signals from the
samples.why: Gastric secretion is partly under nervous control. The smell, sight or thought of food makes the medulla of the brain send messages to the gastric glands, which secrete a small amount of gastric juice even before food arrives.

wrong.1: The pancreas secretes pancreatic juice into the duodenum. It does not send signals to the gastric glands.
wrong.2: The duodenal walls release secretin and CCK, which act on the pancreas and gallbladder after chyme arrives.
wrong.3: The liver produces bile and processes nutrients. It does not send signals that start gastric secretion.

samples.stem: Gas exchange between air and blood occurs by
options: bulk flow through the alveolar wall
samples.why: Gas exchange at the respiratory surface happens by diffusion. Oxygen moves from the air in the alveoli, where its concentration is higher, into the blood, while carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the alveolar air. No energy is spent.

wrong.0: Active transport uses ATP to move substances against a gradient. O₂ and CO₂ simply move down their partial pressure gradients.
wrong.1: Osmosis is the movement of water across a partially permeable membrane, not the movement of gases.
wrong.2: There is no bulk flow of air through the alveolar wall. Individual gas molecules diffuse across the thin, moist membrane.

samples.stem: Inside red blood cells, CO2 combines with water to form carbonic acid in the presence of
samples.why: About 72% of CO₂ travels as bicarbonate. CO₂ enters red blood cells and combines with water to form carbonic acid, CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃, catalysed by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase. Carbonic acid then splits into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻.

wrong.0: Pepsin is a protein-digesting enzyme of the stomach.
wrong.2: Rubisco is a plant enzyme that fixes CO₂ in the Calvin cycle of photosynthesis.
wrong.3: Trypsin is a protein-digesting enzyme from the pancreas, active in the duodenum.

samples.stem: An artificial pacemaker is used in patients with
samples.why: If the SA node is weak or impulses are blocked, the heartbeat may become irregular or stop. Such patients receive an artificial pacemaker, a battery-operated device implanted near the AV node that emits electrical signals to trigger normal beats.

wrong.0: A leaky mitral valve is a valve problem. Damaged valves are corrected by replacing them, not by a pacemaker.
wrong.1: High cholesterol is managed with diet, exercise and medicine. It is not an indication for a pacemaker.
wrong.2: A blocked coronary artery is treated by angioplasty or bypass surgery, not by a pacemaker.

samples.stem: Red bone marrow is found in
options: only the shafts of long bones
spongy bone, ribs, vertebrae, sternum and pelvis
samples.why: Red bone marrow produces red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. It is found in spongy bone, the ends of long bones, ribs, vertebrae, the sternum and the pelvis.

wrong.0: The shafts of long bones are filled with yellow marrow, which is mostly fat.
wrong.1: Cartilage has no marrow. Its matrix does not even contain blood vessels.
wrong.3: Haversian canals carry blood vessels, nerves and lymphatics, not marrow.

samples.stem: The human epidermis is about how many cells thick?
samples.why: The epidermis is the outer layer of the skin and is about 10 to 30 cells thick. Its outermost layer, the stratum corneum, is shed and replaced continuously. This thickness forms a strong barrier against microbes.

wrong.0: 1 to 3 cells would be a very thin lining, like simple epithelium. The skin's epidermis is much thicker.
wrong.2: 100 to 300 cells is far thicker than the epidermis, which is about 10 to 30 cells.
wrong.3: 500 to 1000 cells is far too thick. The epidermis is about 10 to 30 cells thick.

samples.stem: Suppressor T cells cannot stop the cytotoxic attack at first because
options: they are made only in the liver
they multiply more slowly and start in low numbers
samples.why: Suppressor T cells block the cytotoxic T cell response. But they multiply more slowly than cytotoxic T cells and start in low numbers, so at first they cannot stop the attack. After 1 to 2 weeks their numbers rise enough to shut the response down.

wrong.0: T cells develop from bone marrow stem cells and mature in the thymus, not the liver.
wrong.1: Suppressor T cells do work in the specific immune response. Their delay is due to low numbers and slow growth.
wrong.3: Perforins are used against infected or cancer cells. They do not destroy suppressor T cells.

samples.stem: In antibody-mediated immunity, killer cells differ from natural killer cells because they
options: have receptors that recognize antibody-coated antigens
samples.why: Killer cells are similar to natural killer cells, which kill cells by puncturing their membranes. The difference is that killer cells have receptors that recognise antigens already coated with antibodies. When a killer cell meets an antibody-coated cell, it binds and kills it.

wrong.0: Neither killer cells nor natural killer cells make antibodies. Plasma cells make them.
wrong.1: The membrane-attack complex is formed by the final proteins of the complement system.
wrong.2: Pyrogens that trigger fever are released by macrophages, not by killer cells.

samples.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the law of independent assortment?
options: Genes on different chromosomes assort independently
Genes close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together
Alleles of one gene segregate into different gametes
samples.why: The law of independent assortment assumes genes are inherited separately. Genes that lie close together on the same chromosome are often inherited together, a situation called gene linkage. Linkage, crossing over, epistasis, pleiotropy and environment all limit the law.

wrong.0: Genes on different chromosomes assorting independently is exactly what the law predicts, so it is not a limitation.
wrong.2: Alleles of one gene going into different gametes is the law of segregation, which holds true.
wrong.3: Random fusion of gametes at fertilization is assumed in Mendel's predictions. It does not limit the law.

samples.stem: Compared with polygenic inheritance, epistasis usually produces
samples.why: In polygenic inheritance many genes each add a small effect, which gives continuous variation. In epistasis one allele masks or changes the effect of another gene, so offspring fall into a few clear-cut groups. This is discontinuous variation, such as black, brown and yellow Labradors.

wrong.0: Continuous variation is typical of polygenic traits, where many small additive effects blend into a smooth range.
wrong.2: Only intermediate phenotypes are typical of incomplete dominance, where the heterozygote is in between the two parents.
wrong.3: Epistasis changes the expected 9:3:3:1 ratio, for example into 9:3:4 in Labradors or 12:3:1 in foxglove.

samples.stem: In a cross RrYy × RrYy, the book uses the product rule to find the probability of round, yellow offspring. The answer is
samples.why: Each gene can be treated separately. From Rr × Rr, the chance of round is 3/4, and from Yy × Yy the chance of yellow is 3/4. The product rule multiplies independent probabilities: 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16 round, yellow offspring.

wrong.0: 1/16 is the chance of the double recessive, wrinkled green: 1/4 × 1/4.
wrong.1: 3/16 is the chance of round green (3/4 × 1/4) or of wrinkled yellow (1/4 × 3/4), with only one dominant trait.
wrong.3: 3/4 is the chance of only one trait, such as round, without also requiring yellow.

samples.stem: A test cross AaBb × aabb produces offspring in the ratio 42% AaBb, 42% aabb, 8% Aabb and 8% aaBb. What is the distance between genes A and B?
samples.why: In a test cross, the two large classes (42% each) are parental types and the two small classes (8% each) are recombinants. Recombination frequency = 8% + 8% = 16%. Since 1% recombination equals 1 map unit, the genes are 16 map units apart.

wrong.0: 8 counts only one of the two recombinant classes. Both small classes, Aabb and aaBb, are recombinants.
wrong.1: 42% is the size of one parental class, not a recombinant frequency.
wrong.2: 84% is the total of the parental types, 42% + 42%. Map distance is based on recombinants.

samples.stem: The functional units of the ovary, which nurture immature eggs, are the
samples.why: Each ovary contains many tiny sac-like structures called ovarian follicles. They are the functional units of the ovary, because each follicle nurtures an immature egg. Each month one ripening follicle releases its egg at ovulation.

wrong.1: Seminiferous tubules are found in the testes, where sperms are made.
wrong.2: Nephrons are the functional units of the kidney, not the ovary.
wrong.3: The endometrium is the inner lining of the uterus. It does not hold immature eggs.

samples.stem: The human reproductive system differs from other organ systems because it
options: becomes functional only at puberty and differs greatly between males and females
is the same in males and females
is controlled only by the nervous system
samples.why: Most organ systems, such as the digestive or urinary system, are nearly the same in males and females and work from birth. The reproductive system is different in two ways: it is quite different in the two sexes, and it becomes functional only at puberty.

wrong.1: The reproductive system does not work from birth. It matures and starts working at puberty.
wrong.2: The male and female reproductive systems are very different in structure and function.
wrong.3: The reproductive system is controlled largely by hormones such as FSH, LH, testosterone and estrogen, not only by nerves.

samples.stem: The testes lie in the scrotum, outside the abdomen. The scrotum keeps them at about
options: 37 °C, the same as core body temperature
34 °C, slightly below core body temperature, which sperm development needs
samples.why: The testes form inside the abdomen and descend into the scrotum shortly before birth. The scrotum keeps them at about 34 °C, slightly below the core body temperature of 37 °C. This lower temperature is needed for the development of sperms.

wrong.0: 37 °C, the core body temperature, is too warm for normal sperm development. That is why the testes lie outside the abdomen.
wrong.2: 40 °C is above body temperature and would harm sperm development.
wrong.3: 25 °C is far below the temperature the scrotum maintains, which is about 34 °C.

samples.stem: Glycerol, propane-1,2,3-triol, is classified as
samples.why: Alcohols are classified by the number of –OH groups. Those with one –OH are monohydric, and those with more than one are polyhydric. Glycerol, CH₂(OH)CH(OH)CH₂(OH), has three –OH groups, so it is a polyhydric (trihydric) alcohol.

wrong.0: A monohydric alcohol has only one –OH group, such as ethanol. Glycerol has three.
wrong.1: Glycerol has two primary –OH groups and one secondary –OH group, and none that is tertiary.
wrong.2: A phenol has –OH directly on a benzene ring. Glycerol has no ring.

samples.stem: An alcohol with the general formula R₂CHOH is
samples.why: An alcohol is classified by how many alkyl groups are on the carbon carrying the –OH. In R₂CHOH that carbon carries two alkyl groups (R and R) and one H. So it is a secondary (2°) alcohol, like propan-2-ol.

wrong.0: A primary alcohol, RCH₂OH, has only one alkyl group on the C–OH carbon.
wrong.1: A tertiary alcohol, R₃COH, has three alkyl groups and no H on the C–OH carbon.
wrong.3: A phenol has –OH bonded directly to an aromatic ring, not to an alkyl carbon.

samples.stem: Ethanol is a weaker acid than water because
options: ethanol is more polar than water.
the ethoxide ion is stabilized by delocalization.
the ethyl group donates electron density, destabilizing the ethoxide ion.
samples.why: Acid strength depends on how stable the anion is after H⁺ is lost. The ethyl group pushes electron density towards oxygen (+I effect), so the negative charge on ethoxide, CH₃CH₂O⁻, is concentrated and it grabs H⁺ back easily. Hydroxide is less destabilized, so ethanol ionizes less than water and is the weaker acid.

wrong.0: Ethanol is not more polar than water. The difference comes from the alkyl group's effect on the anion.
wrong.1: Ethanol does have an O–H bond. It is the H of this bond that can be lost as H⁺.
wrong.2: Ethoxide has no ring for delocalization. It is phenoxide that is stabilized by delocalization.

samples.stem: Methanoic acid differs from ethanoic acid in that it
options: gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent
samples.why: Methanoic acid, HCOOH, has a hydrogen attached directly to its carbonyl carbon, like an aldehyde. This part is easily oxidized (to CO₂ and water), so methanoic acid acts as a reducing agent and gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. Ethanoic acid has a CH₃ there instead and gives no mirror.

wrong.0: Methanoic acid is a carboxylic acid, so it reacts with NaHCO₃ and gives off CO₂, just like ethanoic acid.
wrong.1: The H of its –COOH group is acidic, so methanoic acid ionizes in water like other carboxylic acids.
wrong.2: Methanoic acid forms esters with alcohols, such as methyl methanoate, like other carboxylic acids.

samples.stem: When ethanal is made by oxidizing ethanol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, the ethanal is distilled off as soon as it forms in order to
options: prevent its further oxidation to ethanoic acid
speed up the reduction of dichromate
samples.why: Acidified dichromate oxidizes ethanol first to ethanal and then on to ethanoic acid. Ethanal has a low boiling point (about 21 °C), so it evaporates as soon as it forms. Distilling it off straight away removes it from the oxidizing agent before it can be oxidized further to ethanoic acid.

wrong.1: Ethanol has the higher boiling point (78 °C), so it stays in the flask to keep reacting. Distillation is not used to remove it.
wrong.2: Distillation protects the product from over-oxidation. It does not speed up the reduction of dichromate.
wrong.3: No hydrate is formed or wanted. The aim is to collect pure ethanal.

samples.stem: During the distillation of ethanal from the oxidation of ethanol, the temperature is kept
options: above the b.p. of ethanal but below that of ethanol
at the b.p. of ethanoic acid
samples.why: Ethanal boils at about 21 °C, lower than ethanol (78 °C). Keeping the temperature above ethanal's boiling point but below ethanol's lets ethanal distil off as soon as it forms, while ethanol stays in the flask to be oxidized.

wrong.0: Below ethanal's boiling point, ethanal would stay in the flask and be oxidized further to ethanoic acid.
wrong.1: Above ethanol's boiling point, the unreacted ethanol would also boil away before it could be oxidized.
wrong.3: At ethanoic acid's boiling point (118 °C), everything would boil off, and the acid is the product to be avoided.

samples.stem: A halogenoalkane is warmed with aqueous ethanolic AgNO₃ and slowly gives a cream-yellow precipitate. The halogen present is
samples.why: Water in the ethanolic solution slowly frees the halide ion, which then forms a silver halide precipitate. The colour identifies the halogen: AgCl is white, AgBr is cream-yellow and AgI is bright yellow. A cream-yellow precipitate means the halogen is bromine.

wrong.1: Chlorine gives a white precipitate of AgCl, and it forms most slowly because the C–Cl bond is strongest of the three.
wrong.2: Iodine gives a bright yellow precipitate of AgI, and it forms fastest because the C–I bond is weakest.
wrong.3: AgF is soluble in water, so no precipitate forms. The very strong C–F bond also hardly breaks.

samples.stem: 2-Chloro-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CCl, is a
samples.why: Halogenoalkanes are classified by the carbon that carries the halogen. In (CH₃)₃CCl, the carbon bonded to Cl is also bonded to three other carbon atoms (the three methyl groups). A carbon joined to three other carbons is tertiary, so this is a tertiary halogenoalkane.

wrong.0: In a primary halogenoalkane, the C–X carbon is bonded to one or no other carbon atoms, as in chloroethane.
wrong.1: In a secondary halogenoalkane, the C–X carbon is bonded to two other carbons, as in 2-chloropropane.
wrong.3: A halogenoarene has the halogen joined directly to a benzene ring. There is no ring here.

samples.stem: Which is a secondary halogenoalkane?
samples.why: A secondary halogenoalkane has the halogen on a carbon that is bonded to two other carbon atoms. In 2-chlorobutane, CH₃CHClCH₂CH₃, the carbon carrying Cl (C-2) is bonded to C-1 and C-3. So it is secondary.

wrong.0: In 1-chloropropane the C–Cl carbon is at the end of the chain, bonded to only one other carbon, so it is primary.
wrong.1: In chloromethane the C–Cl carbon is bonded to no other carbon. It is counted as primary.
wrong.3: In 2-chloro-2-methylpropane the C–Cl carbon is bonded to three other carbons, so it is tertiary.

samples.stem: Which of the following is a free radical?
samples.why: A free radical is an atom or group of atoms with one or more unpaired electrons, which makes it very reactive. In the methyl radical, •CH₃, carbon forms three C–H bonds and keeps one unpaired electron, shown by the dot.

wrong.0: In CH₄ carbon uses all four valence electrons in four C–H bonds, so every electron is paired.
wrong.1: In H₂O all electrons are paired, in two O–H bonds and two lone pairs.
wrong.3: Na⁺ has the neon configuration (2, 8), in which all electrons are paired.

samples.topic: Atomic number, mass number and ions
samples.stem: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are present in the ion ³⁷Cl⁻ (Z = 17)?
samples.why: The number of protons equals the atomic number, Z = 17. Neutrons = A − Z = 37 − 17 = 20. The 1− charge means one extra electron has been gained, so electrons = 17 + 1 = 18.

wrong.1: 16 electrons would give a 1+ ion. A negative ion has gained an electron, so it has 18.
wrong.2: The number of protons is fixed by the element. Chlorine always has 17 protons, not 18.
wrong.3: 37 is the mass number (protons + neutrons). The number of neutrons is 37 − 17 = 20.

samples.topic: Atomic number, mass number and ions
samples.stem: How many electrons are present in the ion ⁵⁶Fe³⁺ (Z = 26)?
samples.why: A neutral iron atom has as many electrons as protons, 26 (equal to Z). The 3+ charge means three electrons have been lost, so Fe³⁺ has 26 − 3 = 23 electrons. The mass number 56 affects only the neutron count.

wrong.0: 26 is the number of protons, or the electrons in a neutral Fe atom. Fe³⁺ has lost three of them.
wrong.1: 29 comes from adding three electrons (26 + 3). A positive ion has lost electrons, not gained them.
wrong.3: 30 is the number of neutrons (56 − 26), not electrons.

samples.stem: According to valence bond theory as described in the textbook, H₂S has a bond angle of about 92° because
options: the two half-filled 3p orbitals of sulfur, which are nearly at right angles, overlap with the 1s orbitals of hydrogen.
the H atoms repel each other strongly.
samples.why: Sulfur (3s² 3p⁴) has two half-filled 3p orbitals, for example 3py and 3pz. Each overlaps with the 1s orbital of a hydrogen atom. Since p orbitals are at right angles to each other, the H–S–H angle stays close to 90°, at about 92°.

wrong.0: sp hybridization would give a linear molecule with a 180° angle, far from 92°.
wrong.1: Sulfur in H₂S does have two lone pairs. The near-90° angle is explained by its use of pure p orbitals.
wrong.3: Strong repulsion between the H atoms would widen the angle, not keep it close to 90°.

samples.stem: According to the Lewis concept, atoms form chemical bonds in order to
options: increase the number of unpaired electrons.
attain a noble-gas electronic configuration, usually an octet.
samples.why: The Lewis concept says atoms combine to complete their outermost shell and reach the stable electronic configuration of a noble gas. For most atoms this means eight electrons in the valence shell, an octet. They do this by losing, gaining or sharing electrons.

wrong.0: Bonding does not change the number of protons or neutrons, so atomic mass stays the same.
wrong.1: Bonding usually pairs up electrons, so it reduces the number of unpaired electrons.
wrong.2: Atoms need not lose all their valence electrons. Many gain or share electrons to complete their shell.

samples.stem: In the formation of sodium chloride, the chloride ion Cl⁻ attains the electronic configuration of
samples.why: Chlorine (2, 8, 7) gains one electron from sodium to form Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8). This is the electronic configuration of argon, the noble gas that follows chlorine. Sodium, by losing its electron, reaches the configuration of neon.

wrong.0: Neon's configuration (2, 8) is reached by Na⁺, not by Cl⁻.
wrong.1: Helium's configuration has only two electrons, but Cl⁻ has 18.
wrong.2: 2, 8, 1 is the configuration of a neutral sodium atom, not of any ion here.

samples.stem: Adding a catalyst to a reversible reaction
options: increases the equilibrium yield of products.
lowers the activation energy for both forward and reverse reactions, so equilibrium is reached sooner without changing its position.
shifts the equilibrium towards the reactants.
samples.why: A catalyst provides a new reaction path with a lower activation energy. It lowers the energy barrier for the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount, so both speed up equally. Equilibrium is reached sooner, but the position of equilibrium, the yield and Kc are unchanged.

wrong.0: A catalyst does not increase the equilibrium yield. It only helps the system reach the same equilibrium faster.
wrong.1: Kc changes only when the temperature changes. A catalyst leaves it unchanged.
wrong.3: Since both directions speed up equally, a catalyst does not shift the equilibrium towards reactants or products.

samples.stem: A buffer contains 0.10 mol dm⁻³ of a weak acid HA (pKa = 4.20) and 0.30 mol dm⁻³ of its sodium salt NaA. The pH is about
samples.why: Using the Henderson equation, pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]) = 4.20 + log(0.30/0.10) = 4.20 + log 3 = 4.20 + 0.48 = 4.68. The salt is in excess, so the pH is above the pKa.

wrong.1: 3.72 comes from using log([acid]/[salt]) = log(1/3) = −0.48, the inverse ratio.
wrong.2: pH = pKa = 4.20 only when the salt and acid concentrations are equal.
wrong.3: 4.50 comes from adding the salt concentration 0.30 directly instead of the log of the ratio.

samples.stem: An irreversible reaction stops when
options: the forward and reverse rates become equal.
the limiting reactant is used up.
samples.why: An irreversible reaction goes in one direction only, turning reactants into products until it is complete. It stops when the limiting reactant, the one present in the smallest required amount, is fully used up, since nothing is left to react.

wrong.0: Equal forward and reverse rates describe dynamic equilibrium, which belongs to reversible reactions, not irreversible ones.
wrong.1: Raising the temperature usually makes a reaction faster. It does not make it stop.
wrong.2: A catalyst only changes the rate of a reaction. It does not cause a reaction to stop.

samples.stem: What mass of copper is deposited from CuSO₄ solution by 1930 C of charge? (Cu = 63.5, F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹)
samples.why: Moles of electrons = charge ÷ F = 1930 ÷ 96 500 = 0.0200 mol. Each Cu²⁺ needs 2 electrons (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu), so moles of Cu = 0.0200 ÷ 2 = 0.0100 mol. Mass = 0.0100 × 63.5 = 0.635 g.

wrong.0: 1.27 g ignores the 2 electrons needed per Cu²⁺ ion, taking 0.0200 mol of copper instead of 0.0100 mol.
wrong.2: 0.318 g comes from dividing the moles of electrons by 4 instead of 2.
wrong.3: 63.5 g is a full mole of copper, which needs 2 × 96 500 = 193 000 C, a hundred times more charge.

samples.stem: In terms of oxidation number, oxidation is
samples.why: Oxidation is the loss of electrons. When an atom loses electrons, its oxidation number rises, for example Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ goes from +2 to +3. So in terms of oxidation number, oxidation is an increase in oxidation number.

wrong.0: A decrease in oxidation number happens when an atom gains electrons, which is reduction.
wrong.1: Gain of electrons is reduction, and it lowers the oxidation number.
wrong.2: If the oxidation number does not change, that atom has been neither oxidized nor reduced.

samples.stem: The oxidation number of sulphur in sodium thiosulphate, Na₂S₂O₃, is
samples.why: In a neutral compound the oxidation numbers add up to zero. Na is +1 and O is −2, so 2(+1) + 2S + 3(−2) = 0. This gives 2S − 4 = 0, so 2S = +4 and S = +2 on average for each sulphur atom.

wrong.1: +4 is the oxidation number of sulphur in SO₂ and sulphites, not in thiosulphate.
wrong.2: +6 is the oxidation number of sulphur in sulphates such as SO₄²⁻ and in H₂SO₄.
wrong.3: −2 is the oxidation number of sulphur in sulphides such as Na₂S.

samples.stem: A sample contains 1.204 × 10²⁴ molecules of glucose. How many moles is this? (Nᴀ = 6.02 × 10²³)
samples.why: Number of moles = number of particles ÷ Avogadro's number. Here n = (1.204 × 10²⁴) ÷ (6.02 × 10²³) = 2 mol. A quick check: 1.204 × 10²⁴ is exactly twice 6.02 × 10²³.

wrong.0: 0.5 mol comes from dividing the wrong way round, Nᴀ ÷ number of molecules. 0.5 mol holds only 3.01 × 10²³ molecules.
wrong.1: 1 mol would contain 6.02 × 10²³ molecules, half the number given.
wrong.3: 12 does not come from dividing by Nᴀ. It is close to the digits 1.204 read without the powers of ten.

samples.stem: 10 cm³ of a gaseous hydrocarbon needs exactly 50 cm³ of oxygen for complete combustion and produces 30 cm³ of carbon dioxide (all volumes at the same temperature and pressure). The hydrocarbon is
samples.why: For gases at the same temperature and pressure, volume ratios equal mole ratios (Avogadro's law). CₓHᵧ + (x + y/4)O₂ → xCO₂ + (y/2)H₂O. CO₂: 30 ÷ 10 = 3, so x = 3. O₂: 50 ÷ 10 = 5 = 3 + y/4, so y = 8. The hydrocarbon is C₃H₈.

wrong.0: C₃H₄ needs 3 + 4/4 = 4 volumes of O₂, which is 40 cm³, not 50 cm³.
wrong.1: C₂H₆ has two carbons, so it gives only 20 cm³ of CO₂, not 30 cm³.
wrong.3: C₃H₆ needs 3 + 6/4 = 4.5 volumes of O₂, which is 45 cm³, not 50 cm³.

samples.stem: One mole of a substance is the amount that contains as many elementary entities as there are atoms in
samples.why: The mole is defined using carbon-12 as the standard. One mole is the amount of substance that contains as many elementary entities as there are atoms in exactly 12 g (0.012 kg) of carbon-12. This number is Avogadro's number, 6.02 × 10²³.

wrong.1: The standard used to define the mole is carbon-12, not hydrogen-1.
wrong.2: The standard used to define the mole is carbon-12, not oxygen-16.
wrong.3: 22.4 dm³ is the molar volume of a gas at STP, not of a liquid, and it is not the basis of the definition.

samples.stem: Catenation is
options: the ability of atoms of the same element to link to each other, forming chains and rings.
the breaking of a C–C bond by heat.
the joining of carbon to hydrogen only.
the formation of ionic bonds by carbon.
samples.why: Catenation (from the Latin catena, meaning chain) is the ability of atoms of the same element to link to each other. Carbon forms very strong, stable C–C bonds, so it can build long chains, branches and rings. This is why there are millions of organic compounds.

wrong.1: Breaking C–C bonds by heat is cracking (thermal cleavage), the opposite of linking atoms together.
wrong.2: Catenation means atoms of the same element bonding to each other. C–H bonds are not self-linkage.
wrong.3: Carbon forms covalent bonds when it catenates. C–C bonds are shared electron pairs, not ionic bonds.

samples.stem: The term "aliphatic" comes from a Greek word meaning
samples.why: Aliphatic comes from the Greek word aleiphatos, meaning fat. Fats contain long open chains of carbon atoms, so open-chain (acyclic) hydrocarbons such as alkanes, alkenes and alkynes are called aliphatic.

wrong.0: Aliphatic compounds are defined by open chains. Ring compounds are called cyclic.
wrong.1: Chain is the meaning of the Latin word catena, which gives the term catenation.
wrong.2: Fragrant is linked to the word aromatic, used for benzene-type compounds.

samples.stem: Cyclohexane is classed as
samples.why: Cyclohexane, C₆H₁₂, is a ring of six carbon atoms joined by single bonds. Alicyclic hydrocarbons are cyclic compounds that behave like aliphatic ones, such as cycloalkanes and cycloalkenes. Cyclohexane reacts much like hexane, so it is alicyclic.

wrong.0: Aromatic hydrocarbons contain a benzene ring or a similar structure. Cyclohexane has no such ring of delocalized electrons.
wrong.1: A heterocyclic ring contains at least one atom other than carbon, such as N or O. Cyclohexane's ring is all carbon.
wrong.2: Cyclohexane is a closed ring with only single bonds. It is neither open-chain nor an alkene.

samples.stem: Duralumin is used for aircraft bodies because it is
samples.why: Duralumin is mostly aluminium (about 93 to 95%) with small amounts of copper, magnesium and manganese. The aluminium keeps it light, the added metals make it much stronger, and it resists corrosion. These properties suit aircraft bodies.

wrong.1: Duralumin is based on aluminium, a light metal, and it is tough rather than brittle.
wrong.2: Duralumin is a metal alloy, so it conducts electricity. It is not an insulator.
wrong.3: Duralumin is a solid at room temperature, which is why it can form an aircraft body.

samples.stem: Chromite, used in stainless steel and pigments, is found in Pakistan at
samples.why: Chromite, an ore of chromium, is found at Muslim Bagh in Balochistan. Chromium is used to make stainless steel and pigments. Other Pakistani deposits are known for different minerals, such as rock salt at Khewra.

wrong.0: Khewra is famous for one of the world's largest rock-salt deposits, not for chromite.
wrong.2: Thar, in Sindh, is known for its large coal reserves, not chromite.
wrong.3: Kalabagh is not the site named for chromite. Chromite is mined at Muslim Bagh.

samples.stem: Gold and platinum are found in the free (native) state because they are
samples.why: Gold and platinum are very unreactive metals. They rarely combine with oxygen, sulfur or other elements, so they are found in nature as the free metal, called the native state. More reactive metals such as Na, Al and Fe exist only in compounds within ores.

wrong.1: Reactive metals form compounds easily, so they are found combined in ores, not free.
wrong.2: Gold and platinum occur as the free metal. Metals such as zinc are found as sulfide ores.
wrong.3: Both gold and platinum are solids at room temperature. Mercury is the only liquid metal.

samples.stem: According to the book, normal blood glucose lies between
samples.why: In a healthy person, the normal blood glucose level is about 70 to 110 mg/dL, with small changes during the day. The hormones insulin and glucagon keep it in this range: insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it.

wrong.1: 7 to 11 mg/dL is ten times too low. Glucose at this level would be far below normal and dangerous.
wrong.2: 700 to 1100 mg/dL is ten times too high. Such levels would mean extreme hyperglycaemia, not a normal value.
wrong.3: 15 to 16 does not match blood glucose. The number 15.6 is the energy from glucose, about 15.6 kJ per gram.

samples.stem: A monomer for addition polymerization must contain
samples.why: In addition polymerization, the π bond of a C=C (or C≡C) bond opens, and the freed electrons are used to link monomers end to end. Without a multiple bond there is nothing to open, so the monomer must contain one, as in ethene, propene or chloroethene.

wrong.1: Two –OH groups make a diol, which forms condensation polymers (polyesters) with dicarboxylic acids.
wrong.2: An –NH₂ and a –COOH group suit condensation polymerization, forming polyamides with loss of water.
wrong.3: A benzene ring alone does not allow addition polymerization. Styrene polymerizes because of its C=C side chain.

samples.stem: Which statement about addition polymerization is correct?
options: The monomers need two different functional groups.
A molecule of water is lost at each step.
All atoms of the monomers end up in the polymer.
It always needs HCl as a catalyst.
samples.why: In addition polymerization, monomers with C=C bonds join one after another in a chain reaction, often started by a free-radical initiator. No small molecule is removed at any step, so every atom of the monomers ends up in the polymer. The polymer has the same empirical formula as the monomer.

wrong.0: Addition polymerization needs a C=C bond. Two functional groups per monomer are needed for condensation polymerization.
wrong.1: Losing a small molecule such as water at each step is the mark of condensation polymerization.
wrong.3: The chain is started by an initiator (or catalyst), such as a free-radical source, not by HCl.

samples.stem: At room temperature, the alkane C₂₀H₄₂ is
samples.why: The physical state of straight-chain alkanes depends on chain length. Those with 1 to 4 carbons are gases, those with 5 to 17 carbons are liquids, and those with 18 or more carbons are waxy solids. C₂₀H₄₂ has 20 carbons, so it is a waxy solid.

wrong.0: Only alkanes with up to four carbons (methane to butane) are gases at room temperature.
wrong.1: Liquid alkanes have 5 to 17 carbons. C₂₀H₄₂ is beyond this range.
wrong.2: Plasma is an ionized state reached only at very high temperatures, not at room temperature.

samples.stem: Complete hydrogenation of benzene gives
samples.why: Complete hydrogenation adds three molecules of H₂ to benzene, one for each double bond in the Kekulé picture: C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₂. It is done over finely divided nickel at about 150 °C and higher pressure. The ring is kept and fully saturated, giving cyclohexane.

wrong.0: Cyclohexene, C₆H₁₀, would form if only one H₂ were added. Complete hydrogenation adds three.
wrong.2: Hexane is an open chain. Hydrogenation saturates the ring but does not break it open.
wrong.3: Cyclohexadiene, C₆H₈, would form if only one H₂ were added to benzene. It still has two double bonds, so it is not fully hydrogenated.

samples.stem: The amide bond of paracetamol is disconnected in retrosynthesis because 4-aminophenol and ethanoyl chloride
options: are known to react by nucleophilic addition–elimination
samples.why: A disconnection should be made at a bond that a known, reliable reaction can form. Amines react readily with acyl chlorides by nucleophilic addition–elimination: the –NH₂ adds to the C=O, then Cl⁻ is eliminated, forming an amide. So disconnecting the amide bond leads to 4-aminophenol and ethanoyl chloride.

wrong.0: 4-Aminophenol is a nucleophile, because of the lone pair on nitrogen. Only the acyl chloride is the electrophile.
wrong.2: No free radicals are involved. The reaction goes through electron pairs.
wrong.3: Acyl chlorides react with amines readily at room temperature. High pressure is not needed.

samples.stem: Butan-2-ol is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid. The main product is
samples.why: Concentrated H₂SO₄ removes the OH and an H from a neighbouring carbon (dehydration). Butan-2-ol can lose H from C1 or C3. Losing it from C3 gives but-2-ene, the more substituted and more stable alkene, so it is the main product (Saytzeff rule). But-1-ene forms only in smaller amounts.

wrong.0: But-1-ene does form, but as the minor product, because it is less substituted and less stable.
wrong.1: Ethers form at lower temperatures with excess alcohol. Under strong heating with acid, the alkene is the main product.
wrong.3: Dehydration removes water and creates a double bond. It does not add hydrogen, so butane is not formed.

samples.topic: Reactions of Na and Mg: oxygen
samples.stem: Which pair correctly matches each metal with the flame seen when it burns in oxygen?
options: Sodium: intense white; magnesium: golden yellow
Sodium: golden yellow; magnesium: intense white
samples.why: Sodium burns in oxygen with a golden-yellow flame, forming a white solid. Magnesium burns with an intense white flame, which is why magnesium powder is used in fireworks and S.O.S. flares.

wrong.0: The colours are swapped. Golden yellow belongs to sodium and intense white to magnesium.
wrong.2: Lilac is the flame colour of potassium and brick red is the flame colour of calcium.
wrong.3: Neither sodium nor magnesium burns with a blue or green flame. Green is typical of barium or copper compounds.

samples.stem: In a Döbereiner triad, chlorine (atomic mass 35.5) and iodine (atomic mass 127) are the first and third members. What atomic mass would Döbereiner's rule predict for the middle member, bromine?
samples.why: Döbereiner grouped similar elements in threes, called triads, and noticed that the atomic mass of the middle element is roughly the average of the other two. For chlorine and iodine this gives (35.5 + 127) ÷ 2 = 162.5 ÷ 2 ≈ 81.3. Bromine's real atomic mass, 79.90, is close to this prediction.

wrong.0: 63.5 is half of iodine's mass alone (127 ÷ 2). The rule averages the first and third members, so chlorine's mass must be added first.
wrong.2: 91.5 is the difference between the two masses (127 − 35.5). The rule needs their average, not their difference.
wrong.3: 162.5 is the sum of the two masses (35.5 + 127). The sum still has to be halved to give the average, 81.3.

samples.stem: What was the main reason Mendeleev's periodic table was accepted as a major success?
options: He arranged the elements in order of increasing atomic number.
He determined atomic numbers using X-ray emission.
He left gaps for undiscovered elements and correctly predicted their properties.
He placed the noble gases in a separate group at the right of the table.
samples.why: In 1869 Mendeleev arranged 63 elements by increasing atomic mass and grouped elements with similar properties together. His real success was that he left gaps for elements not yet discovered and predicted their atomic masses and properties. These predictions proved accurate when the missing elements were later found.

wrong.0: Mendeleev ordered the elements by atomic mass. Ordering by atomic number came later, after Moseley's work in 1913.
wrong.1: Finding atomic numbers from X-ray emission was Moseley's work in 1913, long after Mendeleev's table.
wrong.3: Mendeleev's success is credited to his gaps and correct predictions. The noble gases had not even been discovered when he made his table.

samples.stem: For CHCl₃ + Cl₂ → CCl₄ + HCl, rate = k[CHCl₃][Cl₂]^½. The overall order and the type of reaction that often shows such orders are
samples.why: The overall order is the sum of the exponents: 1 + ½ = 1.5. A fractional order like this is typical of complex reactions that go through several steps. Reactions involving free radicals frequently show fractional orders.

wrong.0: The overall order is 1 + ½ = 1.5, not 2, and fractional orders are linked with free-radical reactions, not ionic ones.
wrong.2: 0.5 counts only the exponent of Cl₂. Photochemical reactions are usually zero order.
wrong.3: The exponents add up to 1.5, not 3, so this is not a third-order (termolecular) case.

samples.stem: According to collision theory, a collision between reactant particles leads to products only if the particles
options: are moving in the same direction.
collide with at least a certain minimum energy and with the proper orientation.
samples.why: Collision theory says that reactant particles must collide to react, but not every collision works. An effective collision needs the particles to have at least a certain minimum energy, the activation energy, and to approach each other with the proper orientation. Otherwise they just bounce apart unchanged.

wrong.0: Equal masses are not a condition for an effective collision. Energy and orientation are what matter.
wrong.1: Collision theory applies to particles in any phase, and reactions in solids are actually slow.
wrong.2: Moving in the same direction does not make a collision effective. Particles need enough energy and the right orientation.

samples.stem: Most chemical reactions are much slower than the rate at which their particles collide. This shows that
options: products are formed before the reactants collide.
activation energy is zero for most reactions.
samples.why: Reactant particles collide extremely often, so if every collision gave products, almost all reactions would be over almost instantly. Most reactions are much slower than this. That shows only a small fraction of collisions are effective, those with enough energy and the correct orientation.

wrong.0: Particles collide very frequently. The problem is that most collisions do not succeed.
wrong.1: Products can form only as a result of effective collisions between reactants.
wrong.2: If activation energy were zero, nearly every collision would succeed and reactions would be very fast.

samples.stem: Which of these liquids has the highest surface tension at 20 °C?
samples.why: Liquids with stronger intermolecular forces have higher surface tension. Water's strong hydrogen bonding gives it 72.75 × 10⁻³ N m⁻¹ at 20 °C. This is far higher than ethanol (22.75), acetone (23.70) and benzene (28.85), in the same units.

wrong.1: Ethanol's surface tension, 22.75 × 10⁻³ N m⁻¹, is only about a third of water's.
wrong.2: Acetone's surface tension, 23.70 × 10⁻³ N m⁻¹, is much lower than water's.
wrong.3: Benzene's surface tension, 28.85 × 10⁻³ N m⁻¹, is much lower than water's.

samples.stem: In NaCl each Na⁺ is surrounded by 6 Cl⁻ ions, but in CsCl each Cs⁺ is surrounded by 8 Cl⁻ ions. The main reason is that
options: Cs⁺ is larger than Na⁺, so more Cl⁻ ions fit around it
Cs⁺ has a larger charge than Na⁺
Cl⁻ is smaller in CsCl than in NaCl
samples.why: Cs⁺ (radius about 167 pm) is much larger than Na⁺ (about 102 pm), while Cl⁻ is the same in both. The larger cation gives a higher radius ratio, r₊/r₋, so eight Cl⁻ ions can fit around each Cs⁺. This gives 8 : 8 coordination in CsCl instead of 6 : 6 in NaCl.

wrong.1: Both Na⁺ and Cs⁺ carry the same +1 charge, so charge is not the difference.
wrong.2: The chloride ion is essentially the same size in both crystals.
wrong.3: CsCl is an ionic crystal made of Cs⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, not separate molecules.

samples.stem: Liquids are less common than solids and gases mainly because
options: the liquid state of a substance exists only within a relatively narrow range of temperature and pressure.
samples.why: Every substance is liquid only between its melting point and its boiling point, and this range is fairly small compared with the conditions on Earth. So the liquid state of any substance exists only within a relatively narrow range of temperature and pressure. That is why liquids are less common than solids and gases.

wrong.0: Liquids do have reasonably strong intermolecular forces. These forces are what keep them from becoming gases.
wrong.1: Liquids are hard to compress, but that property has nothing to do with how common they are.
wrong.3: Liquids are not unstable. They are simply stable over only a limited range of conditions.

samples.stem: The solubility of group 2 hydroxides increases from Mg(OH)₂ to Ba(OH)₂. The book's explanation is that, down the group,
options: hydration energy increases while lattice energy stays constant.
lattice energy decreases more rapidly than hydration energy, so ΔHsol becomes more exothermic.
hydration energy decreases more rapidly than lattice energy, so ΔHsol becomes more endothermic.
both lattice energy and hydration energy increase.
samples.why: Down group 2 the cations get larger, so both lattice energy and hydration energy decrease. For the hydroxides, the lattice energy falls more rapidly than the hydration energy. So ΔHsol becomes more exothermic down the group, and the solubility increases from Mg(OH)₂ to Ba(OH)₂.

wrong.0: Hydration energy decreases down the group as the cations get larger, and lattice energy also decreases.
wrong.2: This describes the sulfates, where hydration energy falls faster and solubility decreases down the group.
wrong.3: Both energies decrease down the group, because the cations get larger.

samples.stem: For a reaction in which the total enthalpy of the products (Hₚ) is less than that of the reactants (Hᵣ), which statement is correct?
options: ΔH is positive and heat is evolved to the surroundings.
ΔH is positive and heat is absorbed from the surroundings.
ΔH is zero because energy is conserved.
ΔH is negative and heat is evolved to the surroundings.
samples.why: The enthalpy change of a reaction is ΔH = Hₚ − Hᵣ. When the products have less enthalpy than the reactants, ΔH is negative. The extra energy is released to the surroundings as heat, so the reaction is exothermic.

wrong.0: A positive ΔH means heat is absorbed, not evolved. Here Hₚ < Hᵣ, so ΔH is negative.
wrong.1: A positive ΔH with heat absorbed needs Hₚ > Hᵣ. That describes an endothermic reaction.
wrong.2: Energy conservation does not make ΔH zero. The enthalpy difference is passed to the surroundings as heat.

samples.stem: Instant cold packs used for injuries contain ammonium chloride and water in separate compartments. They feel cold when kneaded because
options: water freezes when it touches NH₄Cl crystals.
the dissolution of NH₄Cl in water is exothermic.
NH₄Cl reacts with water to release ammonia gas, which is cold.
the dissolution of NH₄Cl in water is endothermic and absorbs heat from the surroundings.
samples.why: Dissolving NH₄Cl in water is endothermic, with ΔH = +16.2 kJ mol⁻¹. When the pack is kneaded, the inner bag breaks and the salt dissolves, absorbing heat from its surroundings. So the pack and anything touching it become cold.

wrong.0: The water does not freeze. The temperature falls because heat is absorbed as the salt dissolves.
wrong.1: An exothermic process releases heat and would make the pack warm, as in a hot pack.
wrong.2: No ammonia gas is released. The cooling comes from the endothermic dissolving of the salt.

samples.stem: The most common geometry for transition metal complexes is
samples.why: Most transition metal complexes have six ligands arranged along the x, y and z axes. Four lie in a square plane at 90°, and the other two sit above and below it. This octahedral shape is the most common, for example [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺ and [Co(en)₃]³⁺.

wrong.0: Linear complexes have only two ligands, as in [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺. They are relatively uncommon.
wrong.1: Square planar shapes are found mainly with d⁸ ions such as Ni²⁺ and Pt²⁺.
wrong.2: Tetrahedral complexes, such as [CoCl₄]²⁻, occur for some ions but are less common than octahedral ones.

samples.stem: Zinc is a d-block element but is not classed as a transition element because
options: its only ion, Zn²⁺, has a completely filled 3d subshell.
samples.why: A transition element must form at least one stable ion with a partly filled d subshell. Zinc is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s², and its only ion, Zn²⁺, is [Ar] 3d¹⁰, a completely filled d subshell. So zinc is a d-block element but not a transition element.

wrong.0: Zinc does have d electrons: ten in its 3d subshell. The problem is that the subshell is full.
wrong.1: Zn²⁺ compounds are usually white, because a full 3d subshell cannot absorb visible light by d–d transitions.
wrong.3: Zinc forms only one ion, Zn²⁺. It does not show variable oxidation states.

samples.stem: Which two first-row transition elements do NOT follow the Aufbau order in their ground-state configurations?
samples.why: Most first-row transition elements fill 4s before 3d as the Aufbau order predicts. Chromium is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and copper is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ instead, because a half-filled d⁵ or a completely filled d¹⁰ subshell is extra stable and more symmetrical.

wrong.0: Mn is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s² and Ni is [Ar] 3d⁸ 4s². Both follow the normal Aufbau order.
wrong.1: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² and Co is [Ar] 3d⁷ 4s². Both follow the normal Aufbau order.
wrong.2: Ti is [Ar] 3d² 4s² and V is [Ar] 3d³ 4s². Both follow the normal Aufbau order.

samples.stem: According to Chapter 12, purified SO₂ and air enter the first converter stage of the contact tower at
samples.why: After purification, SO₂ and air are preheated to 420 to 450 °C and fed into the first converter stage at a pressure of 1 to 2 atm. Here they pass over the V₂O₅ catalyst. This temperature gives a good compromise between rate and yield for the exothermic reaction.

wrong.1: At 25 °C the reaction is far too slow, and a pressure of 200 atm is not used in the contact process.
wrong.2: At 1000 °C the equilibrium yield of SO₃ would be very low, because the reaction is exothermic.
wrong.3: 200 °C and 300 atm are not used. Such high pressure is unnecessary because the yield is already high at 1 to 2 atm.

samples.stem: The electronic configuration of sulfur is
samples.why: Sulfur has atomic number 16 and is in Group 16, period 3. After the neon core (10 electrons), the remaining 6 go into 3s and 3p: [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴. This gives six valence electrons.

wrong.1: [Ne] 3s² 3p⁶ has 18 electrons, which is argon, a noble gas.
wrong.2: [Ar] 4s² 4p⁴ would be a period 4 element. Sulfur is in period 3, and selenium also has 3d¹⁰ electrons.
wrong.3: [Ne] 3s² 3p³ has 15 electrons, which is phosphorus.

samples.stem: Apart from its very strong triple bond, a second reason the book gives for the low reactivity of N₂ is that
options: the N≡N bond is non-polar because both atoms have the same electronegativity.
N₂ is a liquid at room temperature.
samples.why: Besides the very strong N≡N triple bond, N₂ is unreactive because its bond is non-polar. Both atoms are nitrogen with the same electronegativity, so the bonding electrons are shared equally. With no partial charges, there is no site for polar reagents to attack.

wrong.0: N₂ is a covalent molecule held by a triple bond. It has no ions.
wrong.2: Nitrogen has five valence electrons (2s² 2p³), three of which form the triple bond.
wrong.3: Nitrogen is a gas at room temperature. It boils at about −196 °C.

samples.stem: Group 2 elements show similar chemical properties mainly because they all have
options: two electrons in their outermost s subshell (ns²).
samples.why: Chemical properties depend mainly on the outer electrons. Every Group 2 atom has two electrons in its outermost s subshell (ns²). Each loses these two electrons to form an M²⁺ ion, so the elements react in similar ways.

wrong.0: Group 2 elements are s-block elements. Their chemistry is set by the two outer s electrons, not by a filled d subshell.
wrong.2: Seven valence electrons belong to the halogens of Group 17, not to Group 2.
wrong.3: Atomic radius is not the same. The metallic radius rises steadily from Be (112 pm) to Ba (222 pm).

samples.stem: The electron configuration of strontium is
samples.why: Strontium has atomic number 38. The noble gas before it is krypton (36), so two electrons remain and they enter the 5s subshell. Its configuration is [Kr] 5s², which fits the Group 2 pattern of ns².

wrong.1: [Xe] 6s² has 54 + 2 = 56 electrons. That is barium, not strontium.
wrong.2: [Ar] 4s² has 18 + 2 = 20 electrons. That is calcium.
wrong.3: [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s² has 36 + 12 = 48 electrons, which is cadmium. Strontium has only 2 electrons beyond krypton.

samples.stem: The reactivity of Group 2 elements increases from Be to Ba because, down the group,
options: atomic size and shielding increase, so ionization energy decreases.
the number of valence electrons increases.
samples.why: Down Group 2 the atoms get larger and the inner electrons shield the outer ones more. The two outer electrons are held less tightly, so the ionization energy falls and the M²⁺ ion forms more easily. Reactivity therefore rises: Be < Mg < Ca < Sr < Ba.

wrong.0: Ionization energy decreases down the group. The first IE falls from 900 kJ mol⁻¹ for Be to 503 kJ mol⁻¹ for Ba.
wrong.1: Electronegativity decreases down the group, from 1.5 for Be to 0.9 for Ba.
wrong.3: Every Group 2 element has exactly two valence electrons, so that number does not change.

samples.stem:
Choose the correct passive form of:
"The nurse cleaned the wound."
options: The wound is cleaned by the nurse.
The wound was cleaned by the nurse.
The wound has been cleaned by the nurse.
The wound was being cleaned by the nurse.
samples.why: The active sentence is in the simple past (cleaned). In the passive, the simple past becomes was/were + past participle. The object, the wound, becomes the subject: "The wound was cleaned by the nurse."

wrong.0: "Is cleaned" is the simple present passive. The original verb is in the past.
wrong.2: "Has been cleaned" is the present perfect passive. The original is simple past.
wrong.3: "Was being cleaned" is the past continuous passive, which would come from "was cleaning".

samples.stem:
Choose the correct passive form of:
"They are building a new hospital."
options: A new hospital was being built.
A new hospital is being built.
A new hospital has been built.
samples.why: The active sentence is in the present continuous (are building). In the passive, this becomes is/are + being + past participle. The object, a new hospital, becomes the subject: "A new hospital is being built." The doer "by them" is dropped because it is general.

wrong.0: "Is built" is the simple present passive. It loses the idea that building is in progress now.
wrong.1: "Was being built" is the past continuous passive. The original is in the present.
wrong.3: "Has been built" is the present perfect passive, meaning the building is finished. The original says it is still going on.

samples.stem:
Choose the correct passive form of:
"She has written three books."
options: Three books has been written by her.
Three books were written by her.
Three books had been written by her.
Three books have been written by her.
samples.why: The active sentence is in the present perfect (has written). In the passive, this becomes has/have + been + past participle. The new subject "three books" is plural, so have is needed: "Three books have been written by her."

wrong.0: Has is singular, but the new subject "three books" is plural, so it needs have.
wrong.1: "Were written" is the simple past passive. The original is present perfect.
wrong.2: "Had been written" is the past perfect passive, which would come from "had written".

samples.stem: In "The surgeon stitched the wound carefully.", the adverb "carefully" is an adverb of:
samples.why: An adverb of manner tells how an action is done. Carefully answers the question "How did the surgeon stitch the wound?" So it is an adverb of manner. Many adverbs of manner end in -ly.

wrong.1: An adverb of place tells where something happens, such as here or outside. Carefully does not say where.
wrong.2: An adverb of time tells when something happens, such as now or yesterday. Carefully does not say when.
wrong.3: An adverb of frequency tells how often, such as always or rarely. Carefully does not say how often.

samples.stem: In "We will discuss the results tomorrow.", the adverb "tomorrow" is an adverb of:
samples.why: An adverb of time tells when an action happens. Tomorrow answers the question "When will we discuss the results?" So it is an adverb of time, like today, soon and later.

wrong.0: An adverb of manner tells how something is done, such as carefully. Tomorrow does not describe how.
