wrong.2: An adverb of place tells where something happens, such as here. Tomorrow does not say where.
wrong.3: An adverb of frequency tells how often, such as always. Tomorrow refers to a single time, not repetition.

samples.stem: In "He seldom eats fast food.", the adverb "seldom" is an adverb of:
samples.why: An adverb of frequency tells how often an action happens. Seldom means rarely, so it answers the question "How often does he eat fast food?" It is therefore an adverb of frequency, like always, often and never.

wrong.0: An adverb of manner tells how something is done, such as quickly. Seldom does not describe the way he eats.
wrong.1: An adverb of place tells where, such as there or nearby. Seldom says nothing about place.
wrong.3: An adverb of time tells when, such as today. Seldom tells how often, not when.

samples.stem:
Choose the correct indirect form of:
He said, "I am tired."
options: He said that he is tired.
He said that I was tired.
He said that he was tired.
He said that he had tired.
samples.why: When the reporting verb is in the past (said), the tense in the reported words moves one step back: am becomes was. The pronoun I changes to he, to match the speaker. So the indirect form is "He said that he was tired."

wrong.0: The pronoun has changed correctly, but am should shift back to was after the past reporting verb said.
wrong.1: The tense has changed, but the pronoun I should become he, because the speaker is he.
wrong.3: "Had tired" is a different verb meaning, as if he had made someone tired. "Am tired" simply becomes "was tired".

samples.stem:
Choose the correct indirect form of:
She said, "I will come tomorrow."
options: She said that she will come tomorrow.
She said that she would come tomorrow.
She said that I would come the next day.
She said that she would come the next day.
samples.why: In indirect speech after a past reporting verb, will becomes would. Time words also change: tomorrow becomes "the next day" or "the following day". With I changing to she, the indirect form is "She said that she would come the next day."

wrong.0: Will should change to would, and tomorrow should change to the next day.
wrong.1: Will has correctly become would, but tomorrow should change to the next day.
wrong.2: The tense and time word are right, but I should become she, to match the speaker.

samples.stem:
Choose the correct indirect form of:
He said to me, "Where do you live?"
options: He asked me where did I live.
He asked me where I lived.
He said to me where I live.
He asked me where do I live?
samples.why: A reported question uses asked instead of "said to". Question word order (do you live) changes to statement order (I lived), and the tense shifts back from live to lived. You becomes I, since the listener was me. So "He asked me where I lived."

wrong.0: Reported questions do not use did or question word order. "Where did I live" should be "where I lived".
wrong.2: A question is reported with asked, not "said to", and live should shift back to lived.
wrong.3: Reported questions use statement order and end with a full stop. "Where do I live?" keeps question form.

samples.stem: In "The doctor recommended walking every morning," the gerund phrase "walking every morning" is used as:
samples.why: The gerund phrase 'walking every morning' answers the question 'recommended what?'. It receives the action of the verb 'recommended', so it is the direct object of the sentence.

wrong.0: The subject is 'The doctor', who does the recommending.
wrong.2: A subject complement follows a linking verb like 'is'. 'Recommended' is an action verb.
wrong.3: An object of a preposition follows a word like 'in' or 'about'. No preposition comes before this phrase.

samples.stem:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank:
She enjoys ______ detective novels.
samples.why: Some verbs must be followed by a gerund (-ing form), and enjoy is one of them. So the correct form is "She enjoys reading detective novels". Other such verbs include avoid, finish, mind and suggest.

wrong.1: Enjoy does not take a to-infinitive. "She enjoys to read" is a common error.
wrong.2: A bare verb cannot follow enjoy. "She enjoys read" is ungrammatical.
wrong.3: To reading is not used after enjoy. Enjoy takes the -ing form directly.

samples.stem:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank:
He decided ______ medicine after his uncle's illness.
samples.why: Decide is one of the verbs followed by a to-infinitive. So the correct form is "He decided to study medicine". Other verbs like this include plan, hope, want and agree.

wrong.0: Decide does not take a gerund. "He decided studying" is ungrammatical.
wrong.2: Decide needs to before the next verb. A bare infinitive cannot follow it.
wrong.3: To studying wrongly mixes the infinitive marker to with an -ing form.

samples.stem: In "The boy with a red cap is my cousin.", the words "with a red cap" form:
samples.why: "With a red cap" has no subject and finite verb, so it is a phrase, not a clause. It describes the noun boy, telling us which boy is meant. A phrase that describes a noun is an adjective phrase.

wrong.0: An adverb phrase modifies a verb, adjective or adverb. This phrase describes the noun boy.
wrong.1: A noun clause has a subject and finite verb and acts as a noun. "With a red cap" has no verb.
wrong.2: An adverb clause has a subject and finite verb. "With a red cap" has no verb, so it is not a clause.

samples.stem: In "She left the hostel before sunrise.", the words "before sunrise" form:
samples.why: "Before sunrise" has no subject and finite verb, so it is a phrase. It tells when she left, so it modifies the verb left. A phrase that modifies a verb is an adverb phrase.

wrong.1: An adjective phrase describes a noun. "Before sunrise" describes when the action happened, not a noun.
wrong.2: A noun clause needs a subject and finite verb. "Before sunrise" has neither.
wrong.3: An adjective clause needs a subject and finite verb, usually after who, which or that. "Before sunrise" has no verb.

samples.stem: In "I know that he is honest.", the words "that he is honest" form:
samples.why: "That he is honest" has its own subject (he) and finite verb (is), so it is a clause. It answers the question "What do I know?" and acts as the object of know. A clause that acts as a noun is a noun clause.

wrong.0: An adjective clause describes a noun, such as "the man who helped us". This clause is the object of know, not a description.
wrong.2: An adverb clause tells how, when, where or why. This clause tells what I know.
wrong.3: A phrase has no subject and finite verb. This group of words contains "he is", so it is a clause.

samples.stem:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank:
The anatomy exam starts ______ 9 a.m.
samples.why: At is used for a precise point in time, especially clock times. 9 a.m. is an exact clock time, so "starts at 9 a.m." is correct. A memory hook: at for clock times, on for days, in for months and years.

wrong.0: In is used for longer periods such as months, years and parts of the day (in the morning), not exact clock times.
wrong.1: On is used for days and dates, such as on Monday or on 5 May.
wrong.2: By means not later than. "Starts by 9 a.m." would change the meaning to a deadline.

samples.stem:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank:
She was born ______ 2008.
samples.why: In is used with years, months, seasons and other long periods, as in in May or in winter. 2008 is a year, so "She was born in 2008" is correct. A memory hook: at for clock times, on for days and dates, in for months and years.

wrong.1: On is used for days and dates, as in "born on 3 March 2008". A year on its own takes in.
wrong.2: At is used for exact clock times, as in at 5 p.m. It does not go with years.
wrong.3: Since marks a starting point and is used with perfect tenses for continuing actions. Being born is a single past event.

samples.stem:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank:
We will meet ______ Monday.
samples.why: On is used with days of the week and with dates, as in on Friday or on 14 August. Monday is a day, so "We will meet on Monday" is correct. Longer periods take in, and clock times take at.

wrong.0: In is used for longer periods such as months, years and seasons, not for a single day.
wrong.2: At is used for clock times, such as at noon or at 4 p.m.
wrong.3: For shows how long something lasts, as in "for two hours". It does not name a day.

samples.stem:
Choose the correct pronoun:
Everyone except ______ passed the test.
samples.why: 'Except' works as a preposition here, meaning 'but' or 'not including'. A pronoun after a preposition takes the object case, so the correct form is 'Everyone except him passed the test.'

wrong.1: 'He' is a subject pronoun. After the preposition 'except', the object form 'him' is needed.
wrong.2: 'His' is a possessive form, as in 'his book'. It does not fit after 'except' here.
wrong.3: 'Himself' is reflexive and needs a matching subject like 'he' in the same clause. There is none.

samples.stem:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank:
Each of the boys must bring ______ own lunch.
samples.why: Each is a singular indefinite pronoun, so a pronoun referring to it must also be singular, even when a plural noun follows in "of the boys". The group is boys, so the singular masculine form is used. The correct choice is his.

wrong.1: Their is plural. In formal grammar, singular each needs a singular pronoun, and here the gender is known.
wrong.2: Our refers to a group that includes the speaker. The antecedent is each of the boys, not "we".
wrong.3: Its is used for things and animals, not people.

samples.stem:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank:
Neither Sara nor Hina remembered to bring ______ calculator.
samples.why: When two singular nouns are joined by neither...nor, the pronoun that refers to them is singular. Sara and Hina are both female, so the singular feminine possessive her is correct. Her comes before the noun calculator.

wrong.0: Their is plural. Neither...nor joining two singular nouns takes a singular pronoun.
wrong.2: Hers is a possessive pronoun that stands alone, as in "The calculator is hers". It cannot come before a noun.
wrong.3: They is a plural subject pronoun. A possessive form is needed before the noun calculator.

samples.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
samples.why: It's is the contraction of "it is" or "it has". The apostrophe shows where the letter i has been left out. Since the sentence means "It is a beautiful day", "It's a beautiful day" is correct.

wrong.0: Its without an apostrophe is the possessive form, as in "the dog wagged its tail". It cannot mean "it is".
wrong.2: Its' is not an English word. Neither the contraction nor the possessive uses this form.
wrong.3: A comma cannot replace an apostrophe. "It,s" is a punctuation error.

samples.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The two doctor's reports were identical.
The two doctors reports' were identical.
The two doctors' reports were identical.
The two doctors's reports were identical.
samples.why: To show possession with a plural noun that already ends in -s, add only an apostrophe after the s. There are two doctors, so the plural is doctors and the possessive is doctors'. "The two doctors' reports were identical" is correct.

wrong.0: Doctor's is the singular possessive, meaning one doctor. The sentence says there are two doctors.
wrong.1: The apostrophe belongs on the owner, doctors, not on the thing owned. "Reports'" would make reports the owner.
wrong.3: A plural noun ending in -s takes only an apostrophe. "Doctors's" adds an extra s.

samples.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The childrens' ward is on the second floor.
The childrens ward is on the second floor.
The children' ward is on the second floor.
The children's ward is on the second floor.
samples.why: Children is already plural but does not end in -s. Plurals that do not end in -s form the possessive by adding 's, just like singular nouns. So the correct form is children's: "The children's ward is on the second floor."

wrong.0: Childrens is not a word, because children is already plural. The apostrophe is also in the wrong place.
wrong.1: The possessive apostrophe is missing. The ward belongs to the children, so it needs children's.
wrong.2: A plural that does not end in -s needs 's, not just an apostrophe. "Children'" is incorrect.

samples.stem: "Her voice was as smooth as silk." This line uses:
samples.why: A simile compares two different things using "like" or "as". Here a voice is compared to silk with "as smooth as", to show how soft and pleasant it sounds. So the line uses a simile.

wrong.0: A metaphor makes a comparison without "like" or "as", for example "Her voice was silk". This line uses "as".
wrong.1: Personification gives human qualities to something non-human. Here a human voice is compared to silk, so this is not personification.
wrong.2: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration. Calling a voice smooth like silk is a comparison, not an exaggeration.

samples.stem: "When the teacher left, the classroom was a zoo." This line uses:
samples.why: A metaphor says that one thing is another to suggest a likeness. Calling the classroom "a zoo" suggests it became noisy and wild like a zoo, without using "like" or "as". So the line uses a metaphor.

wrong.1: A simile uses "like" or "as", for example "the classroom was like a zoo". There is no such word here.
wrong.2: Onomatopoeia uses words that imitate sounds, such as buzz or bang. No such word appears.
wrong.3: Alliteration repeats the same first consonant sound in nearby words. The line has no such pattern.

samples.stem: "The wind whispered secrets through the pine trees." This line uses:
samples.why: Personification gives human actions or qualities to something that is not human. Whispering secrets is something people do, but here the wind does it. So the line uses personification.

wrong.0: A simile compares two things using "like" or "as". There is no such comparison in the line.
wrong.2: An oxymoron puts two contradictory words side by side, such as "deafening silence". The line has no such pair.
wrong.3: Irony is a contrast between what is said and what is meant, or what is expected and what happens. No such contrast appears.

samples.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: I could not hardly hear him.
samples.why: 'Hardly' already has a negative meaning (almost not). Adding 'not' or '-n't' creates a double negative, which is incorrect in standard English. So the correct sentence is 'I could hardly hear him.'

wrong.0: 'Couldn't hardly' puts two negatives together, the contraction '-n't' and 'hardly'. It is a double negative.
wrong.1: 'Could not hardly' has both 'not' and 'hardly', which is a double negative.
wrong.3: 'Hardly couldn't' is a double negative, and 'hardly' is also in an unusual position before the modal.

samples.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
samples.why: The correct spelling is accommodation, with a double c and a double m. A memory hook: the word is large enough to accommodate two c's and two m's. It means a place to live or stay.

wrong.0: Accomodation has only one m. The correct spelling has a double m: accommodation.
wrong.1: Acommodation has only one c. The correct spelling has a double c: accommodation.
wrong.2: Accommodasion ends in -sion. The correct ending is -tion: accommodation.

samples.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
samples.why: The correct spelling is necessary, with one c and a double s. A memory hook: a shirt has one collar (c) and two sleeves (ss). It means needed or essential.

wrong.1: Neccessary has a double c. The word has only one c: necessary.
wrong.2: Necessery has e before the final ry. The correct ending is -ary: necessary.
wrong.3: Nessesary uses s where c should be. The correct spelling is necessary, with one c and double s.

samples.stem:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank:
Neither the students nor the teacher ______ present.
samples.why: With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it. Here the nearer subject is "the teacher", which is singular. So the singular verb was is correct: "Neither the students nor the teacher was present."

wrong.0: Were is plural and would agree with students, but the verb must agree with the nearer subject, teacher.
wrong.2: Are is plural. The nearer subject, teacher, is singular.
wrong.3: "Have been" is plural. The nearer subject is singular, so it would need "has been".

samples.stem:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank:
The quality of these medicines ______ excellent.
samples.why: The verb agrees with the main subject, not with a noun in a phrase that comes between them. The subject is quality, which is singular; "of these medicines" only describes it. So the singular verb is is correct.

wrong.0: Are agrees with medicines, but medicines is inside the phrase "of these medicines". The subject is quality.
wrong.1: Were is plural and agrees with medicines. The real subject, quality, is singular.
wrong.3: "Have been" is plural. The singular subject quality would need "has been".

samples.stem:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank:
Each of the players ______ a medal.
samples.why: Each is a singular pronoun, even when followed by "of the players". So the verb must be singular, and in the present simple the singular form takes -s. "Each of the players receives a medal" is correct.

wrong.0: Receive without -s is the plural form. Each needs a singular verb.
wrong.1: Are is plural. Each would need is, as in "is receiving".
wrong.2: Have is plural. Each would need has, as in "has received".

samples.stem: Choose the word closest in meaning to ABUNDANT.
samples.why: Abundant means existing in large amounts, more than enough. Plentiful has the same meaning, as in "water is abundant" or "water is plentiful" after the rains. So plentiful is the closest synonym.

wrong.0: Scarce means in short supply, which is the opposite of abundant.
wrong.1: Average means ordinary or typical. It says nothing about something being present in large amounts.
wrong.3: Valuable refers to worth, not quantity. Something can be valuable because it is rare, not abundant.

samples.stem: Choose the word closest in meaning to OBSOLETE.
samples.why: Obsolete means no longer used because something newer has replaced it. Floppy disks, for example, are obsolete. Outdated has the same meaning, so it is the closest synonym.

wrong.0: Modern means new and up to date, the opposite of obsolete.
wrong.1: Broken means damaged and not working. An obsolete machine may still work perfectly but nobody uses it any more.
wrong.2: Costly means expensive. Obsolete is about being out of date, not about price.

samples.stem: Choose the word closest in meaning to LETHARGIC.
samples.why: Lethargic means lacking energy and enthusiasm, slow and drowsy. Sluggish means slow-moving and inactive, so it is the closest synonym. A person often feels lethargic after a heavy meal or during an illness.

wrong.1: Energetic means full of energy and activity, the opposite of lethargic.
wrong.2: Anxious means worried or nervous. A person can be anxious and still very active.
wrong.3: Sleepless means unable to sleep. Lack of sleep may cause lethargy, but the two words do not mean the same thing.

samples.stem:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank:
By next June, she ______ her house job.
samples.why: The future perfect (will have + past participle) describes an action that will be finished before a stated time in the future. "By next June" sets that future deadline. So "she will have completed her house job" is correct.

wrong.0: The simple present completes does not show that the action will be finished before a future point.
wrong.2: Has completed is the present perfect, which looks back from now. It cannot point to a deadline in the future.
wrong.3: Had completed is the past perfect, used for an action completed before a past time. "Next June" is in the future.

samples.stem:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank:
She ______ in Lahore since 2015.
samples.why: Since followed by a starting point (2015) shows an action that began in the past and is still going on. The present perfect, has lived, is used for this. So "She has lived in Lahore since 2015" means she moved there in 2015 and still lives there.

wrong.0: The simple present lives describes a present fact, but it cannot be used with "since 2015" to show duration up to now.
wrong.1: The present continuous is living describes what is happening now. It does not go with since and a starting point.
wrong.2: The simple past lived describes a finished action. Since links the past to the present, so it needs the present perfect.

samples.stem:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank:
By the time we reached the station, the train ______.
samples.why: When two actions happened in the past, the one that happened first takes the past perfect (had + past participle). The train left before we reached the station, so "the train had left" is correct. "By the time" is a common signal for the past perfect.

wrong.1: The simple past left does not make clear that the train went before we arrived. With "by the time", the past perfect is needed.
wrong.2: The present perfect has left links the past to the present. It cannot be used inside a past time frame like "reached".
wrong.3: The simple present leaves describes habits or present facts. It does not fit a story set in the past.

samples.stem:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank:
He studied hard for months; ______, he failed the test.
samples.why: The two ideas contrast: he studied hard, yet he failed. A contrast transition such as however is needed to show this unexpected result. So "He studied hard for months; however, he failed the test" is correct.

wrong.0: Therefore shows a result. Failing is not a logical result of studying hard.
wrong.2: Moreover adds a similar, supporting point. Failing is not an extra point in the same direction.
wrong.3: "For example" introduces an example. Failing the test is not an example of studying hard.

samples.stem:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank:
It rained heavily all morning; ______, the match was cancelled.
samples.why: Heavy rain caused the match to be cancelled. A result transition such as consequently (as a result) is needed to link a cause to its effect. So "It rained heavily all morning; consequently, the match was cancelled" is correct.

wrong.0: However signals contrast. The cancellation is an expected result of rain, not a contrast.
wrong.1: Nevertheless means in spite of that, which signals contrast. There is no contrast here.
wrong.3: "For instance" introduces an example. The cancellation is a result, not an example of rain.

samples.stem:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank:
Regular exercise strengthens the heart. ______, it reduces stress.
samples.why: The first sentence names one benefit of exercise and the second adds another benefit. An addition transition such as moreover (also, in addition) is needed. So "Moreover, it reduces stress" is correct.

wrong.0: However signals contrast. Reducing stress agrees with strengthening the heart, since both are benefits.
wrong.1: "On the contrary" rejects the previous statement. The second sentence supports it.
wrong.2: Otherwise means if not. There is no condition between the two sentences.

samples.stem:
In the sentence below, the word "deft" most nearly means:
"Even after a twelve-hour operation, the surgeon's movements remained deft and precise."
samples.why: Deft means skilful, neat and quick, especially in using the hands. The sentence says the surgeon's movements stayed deft "and precise" even after twelve hours, so the word must describe skilful, controlled movement. Skilful and quick is the closest meaning.

wrong.1: Clumsy means awkward and likely to make mistakes. It is the opposite of deft and does not fit with "precise".
wrong.2: Slow is the opposite of the quickness that deft suggests. The sentence praises the surgeon, it does not criticise them.
wrong.3: Hesitant means unsure and slow to act. Hesitant movements would not be described as precise.

samples.stem:
In the sentence below, the word "scathing" most nearly means:
"Despite the critics' scathing review, the film drew large crowds."
samples.why: Scathing means severely and harshly critical. The word "despite" signals a contrast: the film drew large crowds even though the critics attacked it. A severely critical review is what makes this result surprising.

wrong.0: A highly favourable review would not create the contrast that "despite" signals. Large crowds after a good review would be expected.
wrong.2: Scathing describes the tone of a review, not its length. A short review can be scathing.
wrong.3: Scathing says nothing about how hard a review is to understand. It describes how harsh the criticism is.

samples.stem:
In the sentence below, the word "verbose" most nearly means:
"The speech was so verbose that many listeners lost interest before he reached his main point."
samples.why: Verbose means using more words than are needed, that is, wordy. The sentence says listeners lost interest before the speaker reached his main point, which happens when a speech is padded with unnecessary words. Its opposite is concise.

wrong.0: Verbose is about the number of words, not loudness. A quiet speaker would be described as inaudible.
wrong.1: Verbose does not mean offensive. A speech can be long-winded without insulting anyone.
wrong.3: Short and to the point means concise, which is the opposite of verbose. A concise speech would not lose listeners in this way.

samples.stem:
Statement I: Heavy rain fell in the river's catchment area for a week.
Statement II: The river overflowed its banks.
What is the relationship between the two statements?
options: Statement I is the cause and Statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and Statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of a common cause
The two statements are not causally related
samples.why: A catchment area is the land that drains into a river. A week of heavy rain there pours extra water into the river until it overflows. So Statement I is the cause and Statement II is its effect.

wrong.1: The river overflowing cannot cause rain that fell before it.
wrong.2: There is no separate common cause. The rain itself directly causes the flood.
wrong.3: They are clearly linked, because rain directly raises river levels.

samples.stem:
Statement I: The emergency ward of the city hospital was suddenly crowded.
Statement II: A bus overturned on the motorway near the city.
What is the relationship between the two statements?
options: Statement I is the cause and Statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and Statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of a common cause
The two statements are not causally related
samples.why: When a bus overturns, many passengers are injured and taken to the nearest hospital. That explains why the emergency ward suddenly became crowded. So Statement II is the cause and Statement I is its effect.

wrong.0: A crowded ward cannot make a bus overturn on the motorway.
wrong.2: The accident itself directly explains the crowding, so no separate common cause is needed.
wrong.3: The two are clearly linked, because accident victims are taken to hospital.

samples.stem:
Statement I: Prices of vegetables rose sharply in the markets.
Statement II: Floods destroyed crops across the province.
What is the relationship between the two statements?
options: Statement I is the cause and Statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and Statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of a common cause
The two statements are not causally related
samples.why: Floods that destroy crops reduce the supply of vegetables. When supply falls and demand stays the same, prices rise. So Statement II is the cause and Statement I is its effect.

wrong.0: Higher prices in markets cannot destroy crops in the fields.
wrong.2: The floods directly explain the price rise, so no separate common cause is needed.
wrong.3: Supply and price are closely linked, so the two are related.

samples.stem:
Statement: A pharmacy was found selling expired medicines.
Course of action I: The pharmacy's licence should be suspended until an inquiry is completed.
Course of action II: People should stop buying medicines from all pharmacies.
Which course(s) of action logically follow?
samples.why: Selling expired medicines puts patients at risk. Suspending this pharmacy's licence while an inquiry is done protects the public and is fair, so I follows. Telling people to avoid all pharmacies punishes many for one offender and would stop patients getting medicines.

wrong.1: Avoiding all pharmacies is an overreaction that would harm patients who need medicines.
wrong.2: II does not follow, so both cannot be correct.
wrong.3: I is a proportionate step, so it does follow.

samples.stem:
Statement: Many patients in a district hospital have developed dengue after a week of heavy rain.
Course of action I: The health department should start a drive to remove mosquito breeding sites in the area.
Course of action II: The hospital should be shut down.
Which course(s) of action logically follow?
samples.why: Dengue is spread by mosquitoes, which breed in standing water left by heavy rain. Removing breeding sites tackles the cause of the outbreak, so Course I follows. Closing the hospital would deny care to the very patients who need it, so Course II does not follow.

wrong.1: Shutting the hospital would leave dengue patients without care and make things worse.
wrong.2: II does not follow, because closing the hospital does nothing to stop dengue.
wrong.3: I is a sensible, practical step that attacks the source of the outbreak.

samples.stem:
Statement: A large number of students in one school failed mathematics, while their results in other subjects were good.
Course of action I: The school should review how mathematics is being taught.
Course of action II: All the students should be expelled.
Which course(s) of action logically follow?
samples.why: Students did well in other subjects and failed only mathematics. That points to a problem with how mathematics is taught, so reviewing the teaching follows. Expelling every student is extreme and would not solve the problem.

wrong.1: Expelling all the students is extreme and punishes them for what may be a teaching problem.
wrong.2: II does not follow, because expulsion does not fix the cause.
wrong.3: I is a reasonable step that targets the likely cause.

samples.stem:
"We should appoint Dr Kamal as head of the research lab, because he has published more papers than any other applicant."
Which assumption underlies this recommendation?
options: The number of papers published shows how well someone would run a lab
Dr Kamal has worked at the lab before
The other applicants have never published anything
Research papers are expensive to publish
samples.why: The only reason given for appointing Dr Kamal is that he has published the most papers. That supports the recommendation only if the number of papers shows how well someone would run a lab. This is the hidden assumption.

wrong.1: Previous work at the lab is never mentioned, so the argument does not rely on it.
wrong.2: The argument says he has more papers, not that the others have none.
wrong.3: The cost of publishing papers is irrelevant to choosing the head of the lab.

samples.stem:
"Ali must be a good doctor because he graduated from a famous medical college."
Which assumption does this argument depend on?
options: Ali studied harder than his classmates
Graduates of famous medical colleges are good doctors
Good doctors always work in famous hospitals
samples.why: An assumption is an unstated idea that the argument needs to be true. The argument goes from 'Ali graduated from a famous college' straight to 'Ali is a good doctor'. That jump only works if graduates of famous medical colleges are good doctors, so this is the hidden assumption.

wrong.0: The argument never mentions how hard Ali studied, so it does not depend on this.
wrong.1: Fees have nothing to do with whether Ali is a good doctor. The argument does not rely on cost.
wrong.3: Where good doctors work is not part of the reasoning. The argument is about Ali's college, not hospitals.

samples.stem:
"You cannot trust Dr. Kamal's research on smoking; he is a rude man."
What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: It attacks the person instead of the evidence
It generalises from too few examples
It offers only two choices when more exist
It assumes that what is popular must be true
samples.why: The speaker rejects the research because of Dr. Kamal's manners, not because of any problem with the evidence. Attacking the person instead of the argument is called an ad hominem fallacy. Whether he is rude says nothing about whether his research on smoking is sound.

wrong.1: That describes a hasty generalisation, which draws a broad rule from a few cases. No cases are counted here.
wrong.2: That describes a false dilemma, which offers only two choices. No choices are offered here.
wrong.3: That describes an appeal to popularity. Nothing in the statement mentions what most people believe.

samples.stem: In a row, A is 15th from the left and B is 20th from the right. When they swap places, A becomes 25th from the left. How many people are in the row?
samples.why: When they swap, A moves into B's old seat. So B's seat was 25th from the left, and we know it was 20th from the right. A seat counted from both ends gives total = 25 + 20 − 1 = 44, since that seat is counted twice.

wrong.0: 45 is 25 + 20, forgetting that B's seat is counted from both ends and must be subtracted once.
wrong.1: 40 is 25 + 20 − 5, subtracting 5 instead of 1.
wrong.2: 35 is 15 + 20, using A's old position, which is not the same seat as B's.

samples.stem:
All surgeons are doctors. All doctors are graduates.
Which conclusion must be true?
samples.why: Every surgeon is a doctor, and every doctor is a graduate. So every surgeon falls inside the group of graduates. This chain is a valid syllogism: all surgeons are graduates.

wrong.0: This reverses the statements. Many graduates are not doctors, let alone surgeons.
wrong.2: This may or may not be true in real life, but it does not follow from the statements.
wrong.3: This contradicts the statements, which place every surgeon among the graduates.

samples.stem:
All roses are flowers. Some flowers fade quickly.
Which conclusion must be true?
samples.why: All roses are flowers, but only some flowers fade quickly. The quickly fading flowers may or may not include any roses. Since nothing certain can be said about roses, none of the conclusions must be true.

wrong.0: The quickly fading flowers might all be other kinds of flowers, so this is possible but not certain.
wrong.1: Only some flowers fade quickly, so nothing says that all roses do.
wrong.2: Nothing rules out roses fading quickly, so this cannot be concluded either.

samples.stem:
Five friends, A, B, C, D and E, sit in a row facing north. C sits in the middle. A sits immediately to the left of C. E sits at the right end. B does not sit next to E.
Who sits at the left end?
samples.why: Facing north, left is west. C is in the middle (3rd), A is directly to its left (2nd), and E is at the right end (5th). B and D fill places 1 and 4. B cannot be 4th, next to E, so B is 1st. The order is B, A, C, D, E.

wrong.0: D is in 4th place, next to E, because B is not allowed there.
wrong.1: A sits directly to the left of C, in 2nd place.
wrong.3: E sits at the right end, not the left end.

samples.stem:
Five friends, A, B, C, D and E, sit in a row facing north. C sits in the middle. A sits immediately to the left of C. E sits at the right end. B does not sit next to E.
Who sits between C and E?
samples.why: From the clues, C is 3rd, A is 2nd and E is 5th. B cannot sit next to E, so B is 1st and D is 4th. The order is B, A, C, D, E, so D sits between C and E. Every clue checks: A is directly left of C, E is at the right end, and B is not next to E.

wrong.0: B is at the left end, in 1st place.
wrong.1: A is to the left of C, in 2nd place.
wrong.2: C is 3rd and E is 5th, so there is one seat between them, taken by D.

samples.stem:
Sara is twice as old as Ali. In 5 years, the sum of their ages will be 40.
How old is Ali now?
samples.why: Let Ali's age be x, so Sara's is 2x. In 5 years their ages will be x + 5 and 2x + 5. Their sum is 3x + 10 = 40, so 3x = 30 and x = 10. Check: Ali 15 and Sara 25 in five years, which add to 40.

wrong.1: If Ali were 15, Sara would be 30. In five years they would be 20 and 35, a sum of 55.
wrong.2: If Ali were 12, Sara would be 24. In five years they would be 17 and 29, a sum of 46.
wrong.3: 20 is Sara's present age, not Ali's.

samples.stem:
What comes next in the series?
2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, ?
samples.why: These are prime numbers in order. A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself. After 13, the number 14 is even, 15 = 3 × 5 and 16 is even, so the next prime is 17.

wrong.1: 15 is not prime because 15 = 3 × 5, so it has factors other than 1 and itself.
wrong.2: 19 is prime, but it skips 17, which comes first.
wrong.3: 16 is not prime. It is even, so it divides by 2.

samples.stem:
What comes next in the series?
2, 6, 18, 54, ?
samples.why: Each term is 3 times the one before: 2 × 3 = 6, 6 × 3 = 18, 18 × 3 = 54. The next term is 54 × 3 = 162. This is a geometric series with a common ratio of 3. A quick check: 162 ÷ 54 = 3, the same ratio as every earlier step.

wrong.1: 108 is 54 × 2. The series multiplies by 3, not 2.
wrong.2: 72 is 54 + 18, adding the previous term. The rule is to multiply by 3.
wrong.3: 216 is 54 × 4. The multiplier stays 3, it does not grow.

samples.stem:
What comes next in the series?
3, 7, 15, 31, 63, ?
samples.why: Each term is double the previous one plus 1: 3 × 2 + 1 = 7, 7 × 2 + 1 = 15, 15 × 2 + 1 = 31, 31 × 2 + 1 = 63. So the next is 63 × 2 + 1 = 127. The gaps 4, 8, 16, 32 also double, and 63 + 64 = 127.

wrong.0: 126 is 63 × 2. It forgets to add 1, which every step of the series does.
wrong.2: 95 is 63 + 32, repeating the last gap. The gaps double each time, so the next gap is 64.
wrong.3: 125 is 63 × 2 − 1. The rule adds 1, it does not subtract 1.

samples.stem: An alternating current is one that
options: varies sinusoidally and reverses its direction every half-cycle
flows in one direction with a constant value
flows in one direction but in pulses
samples.why: An alternating current varies with time as a sine (or cosine) function. It rises to a peak, falls to zero, reverses direction to a negative peak and returns, so its direction reverses every half-cycle. The peak value is the same in every cycle.

wrong.1: A current that flows in one direction with a constant value is direct current (DC).
wrong.2: Current in one direction in pulses is pulsating DC, such as the output of a rectifier.
wrong.3: A current that keeps increasing never reverses, so it is not alternating.

samples.stem: The mains supply in Pakistan has a frequency of 50 Hz. What is its time period?
samples.why: The time period is the reciprocal of frequency: T = 1/f = 1 ÷ 50 Hz = 0.02 s. Since 1 ms = 10⁻³ s, this is 20 ms. So the mains supply completes 50 full cycles every second, each lasting 20 ms.

wrong.0: 50 ms would be the period of a 20 Hz supply, since 1 ÷ 0.05 s = 20 Hz.
wrong.2: 2 ms would be the period of a 500 Hz supply, since 1 ÷ 0.002 s = 500 Hz.
wrong.3: 0.5 s would be the period of a 2 Hz supply, far slower than the mains.

samples.stem: During one cycle of a sinusoidal alternating voltage, where does the voltage change most rapidly?
options: It changes at the same rate throughout.
samples.why: The rate of change of a sine wave is given by the steepness of its graph. The curve is steepest where it crosses zero, so the voltage changes most rapidly at the zero (crossover) points. At the peaks the curve is momentarily flat, so the change is slowest there.

wrong.0: At the positive peak the curve is momentarily flat, so the voltage changes most slowly there.
wrong.1: The negative peak is also a flat turning point, so the voltage changes most slowly there too.
wrong.3: The slope of a sine curve changes continuously, from steepest at zero to flat at the peaks.

samples.stem: A turntable rotates at 45 rpm. Its angular velocity is about:
samples.why: First change to revolutions per second: f = 45 ÷ 60 = 0.75 rev s⁻¹. Each revolution is 2π rad, so ω = 2πf = 2π × 0.75 ≈ 4.7 rad s⁻¹. In general, to change rpm to rad s⁻¹, multiply by 2π and divide by 60.

wrong.0: 0.75 is the frequency in revolutions per second. It must be multiplied by 2π to give radians per second.
wrong.2: 45 is the speed in revolutions per minute. It needs converting to radians per second.
wrong.3: About 283 comes from multiplying 45 by 2π without first dividing by 60 to change minutes to seconds.

samples.stem: A spinning gyroscope keeps the direction of its axis because:
options: it has no moment of inertia
gravity does not act on a spinning object
friction locks its axis in place
its large angular momentum can be changed in direction only by a large torque
samples.why: A gyroscope is a fast-spinning flywheel mounted in supporting rings. Spinning at high speed gives it a large angular momentum, and changing the direction of that angular momentum needs a correspondingly large torque. Without such a torque its axis keeps the same direction, which is why gyroscopes help navigate aeroplanes, ships and spacecraft.

wrong.0: A gyroscope has a large moment of inertia, not zero. Its large I and high spin rate together give it large angular momentum.
wrong.1: Gravity acts on every object with mass, spinning or not. The gyroscope keeps its orientation because of its angular momentum, not because gravity is absent.
wrong.2: The gyroscope is mounted in rings so that it can turn freely. Friction does not lock its axis; its angular momentum keeps the axis steady.

samples.stem: One radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length is:
options: equal to the radius of the circle
equal to the diameter of the circle
samples.why: The radian is defined using arc length: one radian is the angle at the centre of a circle subtended by an arc equal in length to the radius. In general θ = S/r, so S = r gives θ = 1 rad. It is the SI unit of angle.

wrong.1: An arc equal to the diameter is 2r long, so it subtends 2 rad, not 1 rad.
wrong.2: The whole circumference, 2πr, subtends 2π rad, which is one full revolution.
wrong.3: A quarter of the circumference subtends 2π/4 = π/2 rad, which is 90°.

samples.stem: Carbon fibres embedded in a concrete bridge carry a small current. Over time, the measured resistance of the fibre network increases. This suggests that:
options: the fibres have become better conductors
the concrete is cracking and the fibres are separating
samples.why: Carbon fibres embedded in the concrete slab form a conducting network. If its resistance stays steady over time, the bridge is keeping its structural strength. A rising resistance means the concrete is deteriorating or the fibres are being damaged, for example by cracks pulling them apart.

wrong.0: A stronger bridge would leave the fibre network intact, so its resistance would stay the same, not increase.
wrong.1: The rising resistance is used as a sign of damage to the structure, not as a measure of cooling.
wrong.2: If the fibres became better conductors, the network's resistance would fall, not rise.

samples.stem: A charge of 90 C passes through a cross-section of a wire in 1 minute. The current is:
samples.why: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q/t, with time in seconds. One minute is 60 s, so I = 90 C ÷ 60 s = 1.5 A. One ampere means one coulomb of charge passing each second.

wrong.0: 0.67 is 60 ÷ 90, which divides the time by the charge. Current is charge divided by time.
wrong.2: 90 A treats the time as 1 s. One minute is 60 s.
wrong.3: 5400 multiplies the charge by the time. Current divides the charge by the time.

samples.stem: A bulb lights almost at once when switched on, even though the drift velocity of electrons is very small. This is because:
options: electrons from the switch travel to the bulb at the speed of light
the bulb stores electrons, ready to release them
all the free electrons in the circuit start drifting at once, and the disturbance travels along the wire almost instantly
the drift velocity becomes very large at the moment of switching
samples.why: A wire is already full of free electrons. When the switch is closed, an electric field is set up along the whole circuit almost at once, so all the free electrons start drifting together, including those inside the bulb. Each electron moves slowly, but the bulb lights almost immediately.

wrong.0: Individual electrons drift very slowly, around 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹. They do not travel from the switch to the bulb at the speed of light.
wrong.1: A bulb does not store electrons. The electrons already in its filament start moving when the circuit is closed.
wrong.3: The drift velocity stays small at all times. The quick response comes from all the electrons moving together.

samples.stem: In a loudspeaker, ferrofluid held around the voice coil is used to:
options: make the coil a permanent magnet
increase the electrical resistance of the coil
cool the coil and damp unwanted vibrations
samples.why: The voice coil of a loudspeaker heats up while it works. The speaker's magnetic field holds ferrofluid in place around the coil, where it absorbs and carries away heat. It also damps unwanted vibrations, which improves sound quality.

wrong.0: Ferrofluid particles are only temporarily magnetised, and the voice coil is an electromagnet driven by current, not a permanent magnet.
wrong.1: Raising the coil's resistance is not its purpose. Ferrofluid is used for cooling and damping.
wrong.2: Ferrofluid does not store electrical energy. That is the job of a capacitor or battery.

samples.stem: Mutual induction is the production of an emf in one coil
options: by a changing current in a neighbouring coil
by a steady current in the same coil
samples.why: When the current in one coil (the primary) changes, the magnetic flux it produces changes. This changing flux links a neighbouring coil (the secondary) and induces an emf in it. This is mutual induction, the principle behind the transformer.

wrong.1: An emf from a changing current in the same coil is self-induction, and a steady current induces nothing.
wrong.2: Heating a neighbouring coil does not induce an emf. A changing magnetic flux is needed.
wrong.3: A constant magnetic field gives no change of flux, so it induces no emf.

samples.stem: The current in a primary coil changes at 40 A s⁻¹. If the mutual inductance between the coils is 0.50 H, what emf is induced in the secondary?
samples.why: The emf induced in the secondary coil is proportional to the rate of change of current in the primary: ε_s = M ΔI_p/Δt. Substituting: ε_s = 0.50 H × 40 A s⁻¹ = 20 V. A steady primary current would induce no emf at all.

wrong.0: 80 V comes from dividing 40 by 0.50 instead of multiplying by the mutual inductance.
wrong.2: 0.0125 V comes from dividing M by the rate of change of current, which inverts the formula.
wrong.3: 40 V uses the rate of change of current alone and leaves out the mutual inductance M.

samples.topic: Charged particle in a magnetic field
samples.stem: A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field at right angles to it and moves in a circle of radius r. If its speed is doubled, the radius becomes
samples.why: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r. This gives r = mv/(qB), so with m, q and B fixed the radius is directly proportional to the speed. Doubling v doubles the radius to 2r.

wrong.0: r/2 would mean a faster particle bends more sharply. In fact r = mv/qB grows with speed.
wrong.1: The radius does depend on speed, since r = mv/qB. Only the period stays the same.
wrong.2: 4r treats r as proportional to v². The formula r = mv/qB shows r ∝ v.

samples.stem: The link between electricity and magnetism was first discovered in 1820, when it was found that a current produces a magnetic field. This was discovered by:
samples.why: In 1820 Hans Christian Oersted noticed that a current-carrying wire deflects a nearby compass needle. This showed that an electric current produces a magnetic field, the first link found between electricity and magnetism.

wrong.0: Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831, the reverse effect, where a changing magnetic field produces a current.
wrong.1: Heinrich Lenz gave the rule (1834) for the direction of an induced current. He did not discover the magnetic effect of current.
wrong.2: Charles de Coulomb measured the force between electric charges. That is electrostatics, not electromagnetism.

samples.stem: Lodestone, the natural mineral that led to the invention of the compass, is the iron oxide:
samples.why: Lodestone is naturally magnetised magnetite, an iron oxide with formula Fe₃O₄. It attracts iron and steel and lines up with the Earth's magnetic poles, which led to the invention of the compass.

wrong.0: Haematite, Fe₂O₃, is a common iron ore but it is only weakly magnetic. It is not lodestone.
wrong.1: Iron pyrite, FeS₂, is an iron sulphide (fool's gold), not an oxide, and it is not lodestone.
wrong.2: Rust is hydrated iron oxide formed by corrosion. It is not the natural magnetic mineral lodestone.

samples.stem: Rectification is the process of
options: converting alternating current into direct current
converting direct current into alternating current
samples.why: Rectification is the process of converting alternating current into direct current. It uses diodes, which conduct in only one direction, so current through the load flows one way only. The result is a unidirectional current that can be smoothed into steady DC.

wrong.1: Converting DC into AC is done by an inverter, the reverse of rectification.
wrong.2: Increasing the voltage of AC is the job of a step-up transformer.
wrong.3: Storing charge is what a capacitor does. It is not rectification.

samples.stem: In a half-wave rectifier with one diode and a load resistor,
options: current flows through the load during both halves of the cycle
current flows through the load only during one half of each input cycle
no current ever flows through the load
the output is a smooth, steady DC
samples.why: In one half-cycle the diode is forward biased and conducts, so current flows through the load. In the other half-cycle it is reverse biased and blocks the current. The output is pulsating DC with a gap in every other half-cycle.

wrong.0: Current through the load in both halves of the cycle happens in full-wave rectification.
wrong.2: The diode does conduct during the half-cycle in which it is forward biased.
wrong.3: Without a smoothing capacitor, the output is a series of pulses, not a smooth, steady DC.

samples.stem: In a full-wave bridge rectifier, how many diodes conduct during each half-cycle of the input?
samples.why: A bridge rectifier has four diodes arranged in two pairs. In each half-cycle one pair is forward biased and conducts in series through the load, while the other pair is reverse biased and blocks. So two diodes conduct at a time, and the current through the load is always in the same direction.

wrong.0: Only one diode conducting is the case for a half-wave rectifier.
wrong.1: The diodes work in pairs, so three cannot conduct together.
wrong.3: Only one pair conducts at a time. The other pair is reverse biased and blocks.

samples.stem: The capacitance of an isolated spherical conductor is defined as
options: the charge stored on it per unit potential at its surface
the potential at its surface per unit charge
the charge stored per unit radius
the energy stored per unit charge
samples.why: The capacitance of an isolated sphere is the charge on it per unit electric potential at its surface: C = Q/V. Its unit is the farad (1 F = 1 C V⁻¹). A larger capacitance means more charge can be stored for each volt of potential.

wrong.1: Potential per unit charge, V/Q, is the reciprocal of capacitance.
wrong.2: Capacitance is charge per volt, not charge per unit radius.
wrong.3: Energy per unit charge is a potential, measured in volts, not a capacitance.

samples.stem: A conducting sphere of radius 10 cm carries a charge of 2 nC. The electric field at a point 30 cm from its centre is (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²):
samples.why: Outside a charged conducting sphere, Gauss's law shows the field is the same as if all the charge were at the centre: E = kq/r², with r measured from the centre. Here E = 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁹ ÷ (0.3)² = 18 ÷ 0.09 = 200 N C⁻¹.

wrong.0: 60 N C⁻¹ is 18 ÷ 0.3, dividing by r instead of r².
wrong.2: 450 N C⁻¹ uses r = 0.2 m, the distance from the surface. The distance must be measured from the centre, 0.3 m.
wrong.3: 1800 N C⁻¹ uses r = 0.1 m, the radius of the sphere, which gives the field at its surface, not at 30 cm.

samples.stem: At the midpoint between two equal positive point charges,
options: the potential is zero but the electric field is not
the electric field is zero but the potential is not
both the field and the potential are zero
neither the field nor the potential is zero
samples.why: Electric field is a vector. At the midpoint the two equal fields point in opposite directions, so they cancel and E = 0. Potential is a scalar, so the two positive potentials add: V = 2kq/(d/2) = 4kq/d, which is not zero.

wrong.0: Zero potential with a non-zero field is the situation midway between equal and opposite charges.
wrong.2: The field cancels, but potential is a scalar, and two positive potentials add instead of cancelling.
wrong.3: The fields do cancel at the midpoint, because they are equal and opposite there.

samples.stem: A small steel ball falls through oil at a terminal velocity of 2 cm s⁻¹. A ball of the same steel with twice the radius would have a terminal velocity of
samples.why: At terminal velocity the drag balances the weight minus upthrust. Weight and upthrust grow with volume, ∝ r³, while Stokes's drag 6πηrv grows with r. So r³ ∝ rv, giving v ∝ r². Doubling the radius makes the terminal velocity 4 × 2 = 8 cm s⁻¹.

wrong.0: 4 cm s⁻¹ assumes v ∝ r. The weight grows as r³ and the drag as r, so v ∝ r².
wrong.1: 2.8 cm s⁻¹ (2√2) assumes v ∝ √r, which has no basis here.
wrong.2: 16 cm s⁻¹ assumes v ∝ r³, forgetting that the drag also grows with the radius.

samples.stem: In streamline (laminar) flow:
options: the particles move in eddies and whirlpools
the velocity at each point changes abruptly
every particle passing a point follows the same path as the particles that passed it earlier
samples.why: In streamline or laminar flow the motion is smooth and steady. Every particle that passes a given point follows exactly the same path as the particles that passed that point earlier. These paths are called streamlines, and two streamlines can never cross.

wrong.0: Eddies and whirlpools are features of turbulent flow, where the particles' paths keep changing.
wrong.1: If streamlines crossed, a particle at the crossing would have two directions at once. In streamline flow they never cross.
wrong.2: Abrupt changes of velocity at a point happen in turbulent flow. In streamline flow the velocity at each point stays steady.

samples.stem: Fluid flow becomes turbulent when:
options: the flow speed rises above a certain value
the flow speed is very small
samples.why: A fluid flows smoothly as long as its speed is low. Above a certain speed the motion becomes irregular and unsteady, with eddies and whirlpools, and the velocity at a point changes abruptly. This is turbulent flow.

wrong.1: A fluid at rest is not flowing at all, so it cannot have turbulent flow.
wrong.2: Very slow flow tends to be smooth and streamlined. Turbulence appears at higher speeds.
wrong.3: Zero viscosity describes an ideal fluid, which is assumed to flow smoothly. Turbulence is linked to high speed, not to the absence of viscosity.

samples.stem: For an elastic collision in two dimensions, the book applies conservation of momentum:
options: only along the direction of the first ball
separately along the x-axis and the y-axis, together with conservation of kinetic energy
by adding the magnitudes of all momenta
samples.why: Momentum is a vector, so in two dimensions it is resolved into rectangular components. The total x-momentum and the total y-momentum are each conserved separately. Because the collision is elastic, conservation of kinetic energy, a scalar, gives one more equation.

wrong.0: Momentum must be conserved in both perpendicular directions. Using only the first ball's direction ignores the sideways motion.
wrong.2: Momentum is a vector, so magnitudes cannot simply be added. It must be split into components.
wrong.3: For an elastic collision, conservation of kinetic energy is an essential extra equation.

samples.stem: A 4 kg block on a horizontal table (μk = 0.2) is tied by a string over a light frictionless pulley to a hanging 1 kg mass. Once moving, the acceleration of the system is (g = 10 m s⁻²)
samples.why: The hanging mass pulls with its weight, 1 × 10 = 10 N. Kinetic friction on the block is μkN = 0.2 × 4 × 10 = 8 N. The net force moves both masses: a = (10 − 8)/(4 + 1) = 0.4 m s⁻².

wrong.0: 2.0 m s⁻² is 10/5, which ignores the 8 N of friction on the table.
wrong.1: 1.6 m s⁻² divides the friction force by the total mass. The net force is 10 − 8 = 2 N.
wrong.2: The pull of 10 N is larger than the 8 N of friction, so there is a net force and the system accelerates.

samples.stem: The equations of motion apply only to bodies moving:
options: in a circle with constant speed
only when they start from rest
in a straight line with constant acceleration
samples.why: The three equations of motion, such as v_f = v_i + at, were derived assuming the acceleration stays constant and the body moves along a straight line. So they can only be applied to objects moving in a straight line with constant acceleration.

wrong.0: In circular motion the direction keeps changing, so the acceleration is not constant in direction. The straight-line equations do not apply.
wrong.1: The equations are derived for constant acceleration. If the acceleration varies, they give wrong results.
wrong.2: The equations include an initial velocity v_i, so the body does not need to start from rest.

samples.stem: A radioactive tracer is useful because
options: it is chemically completely different from the normal element
it behaves chemically like the normal isotope, but its location can be followed by detecting the radiation it emits
it emits no radiation inside the body
it makes the body produce more of the element
samples.why: A radioactive isotope has the same number of protons and electrons as the stable isotope, so it takes part in exactly the same chemical and biological processes. The difference is that it emits radiation, so detectors outside the body or system can follow where it goes and how much collects there.

wrong.0: A tracer must behave chemically like the normal element. If it behaved differently, it would not follow the normal process being studied.
wrong.2: A tracer is useful only because it emits radiation that detectors can pick up. Without radiation its path could not be followed.
wrong.3: A tracer only marks where the element goes. It is given in tiny amounts and does not make the body produce more of anything.

samples.stem: Radioactive decay is described as random because
options: it is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or when; only the probability of decay per unit time (the decay constant) is fixed
all nuclei decay at the same moment
decay depends on the size of the sample
samples.why: Each nucleus has a fixed chance of decaying in each second, called the decay constant λ. It is impossible to say which nucleus will decay next or exactly when. With very large numbers of nuclei, though, the overall rate A = λN is predictable, which is why the half-life is constant.

wrong.1: Nuclei do not all decay together. They decay one by one at unpredictable times.
wrong.2: The half-life of a given nuclide is a fixed constant. It is the individual decays that are random.
wrong.3: The chance of decay per nucleus is the same whatever the sample size. A bigger sample just has more decays per second.

samples.stem: According to Max Planck's quantum theory, energy is radiated or absorbed
options: in discrete packets (quanta), each of energy E = hf
only by charged particles at rest
in packets whose energy depends only on the intensity
samples.why: In 1901 Max Planck proposed that radiation is not emitted or absorbed continuously but in separate packets called quanta. The energy of each quantum is proportional to its frequency: E = hf, where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is Planck's constant.

wrong.0: Continuous emission in any amount is the classical idea that Planck's theory replaced.
wrong.2: Radiation is emitted by accelerated, oscillating charges, not by charges at rest.
wrong.3: Each quantum's energy depends on its frequency, E = hf. Intensity only sets how many quanta there are.

samples.stem: Which of these is an example of an irreversible process?
options: Slow evaporation and condensation of a liquid
Very slow compression of a gas in a cylinder
samples.why: Any change that happens suddenly, or involves friction or loss of energy by conduction, convection or radiation, cannot be retraced and is irreversible. An explosion is a highly irreversible process: the burnt gases and released heat cannot be turned back into the original explosive.

wrong.0: Evaporation and condensation carried out slowly can be run backwards through the same stages, so they are practically reversible.
wrong.2: A gas compressed very slowly can be expanded again by slowly reducing the pressure, so this is nearly reversible.
wrong.3: Slow liquefaction can be reversed by slow evaporation, so it is practically reversible.

samples.stem: Which is one of the assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases?
options: Gas molecules attract each other strongly at all distances.
The volume of the molecules is a large part of the gas volume.
Gas molecules are at rest unless heated.
The collisions between gas molecules and with the walls are perfectly elastic.
samples.why: The kinetic theory assumes that gas molecules collide with each other and with the container walls perfectly elastically, so no kinetic energy is lost overall. It also assumes constant random motion, negligible molecular volume and no forces between molecules except during collisions.

wrong.0: The theory assumes there are no attractive or repulsive forces between molecules, except during collisions.
wrong.1: The volume of the molecules is assumed to be negligible compared with the volume of the gas, so they act like points.
wrong.2: Gas molecules are always in constant, random motion. They are not at rest when the gas is cool.

samples.stem: According to the kinetic theory, the pressure of a gas on the walls of its container is due to:
options: collisions of the gas molecules with the walls
the weight of the gas pressing down
attraction between molecules and the walls
samples.why: Gas molecules constantly strike the walls of their container and bounce back. Each collision changes a molecule's momentum, so it exerts a small force on the wall. The total force per unit area from all these collisions is the gas pressure.

wrong.1: Gas pressure acts equally on all the walls, including the top and sides. The weight of the gas would only press on the bottom.
wrong.2: The kinetic theory assumes no attraction between molecules and the walls. Pressure comes from collisions.
wrong.3: The volume of the molecules is assumed to be negligible, so it cannot be the cause of pressure.

samples.stem: A vector has components Aₓ = 5 units and A_y = 5√3 units. The angle it makes with the x-axis is:
samples.why: The angle with the x-axis is θ = tan⁻¹(A_y ÷ Aₓ). Here A_y ÷ Aₓ = 5√3 ÷ 5 = √3, and tan 60° = √3, so θ = 60°. Both components are positive, so the vector lies in the first quadrant.

wrong.0: tan 30° = 1/√3, which would need A_y = Aₓ/√3. Here the ratio is √3, giving 60°.
wrong.1: 45° needs the two components to be equal, so that tan θ = 1.
wrong.3: 90° would need Aₓ = 0, with the vector pointing straight along the y-axis.

samples.stem: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
samples.why: A scalar is a quantity fully described by its magnitude, a number and a unit, with no direction. Energy is the capacity to do work, and 25 J of energy needs no direction to describe it. Mass, distance, speed, time and temperature are other scalars.

wrong.1: Displacement is the change in position and needs a direction, for example 10 m towards west, so it is a vector.
wrong.2: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity and has a direction, for example 10 m s⁻² upward, so it is a vector.
wrong.3: Force is a push or pull that acts in a definite direction, for example 20 N to the right, so it is a vector.

samples.stem: Which group contains only vector quantities?
samples.why: Vectors need both magnitude and direction to describe them fully. Displacement (change in position in a direction), velocity (speed in a given direction) and force (a push or pull in a direction) are all vectors. Every other group contains at least one scalar.

wrong.0: Distance, speed and time are all described by magnitude alone, so they are scalars.
wrong.1: Mass, energy and temperature are all scalars, with no direction needed.
wrong.2: Velocity and acceleration are vectors, but speed is a scalar, so this group is mixed.

samples.stem: When x = x₀ cos ωt, the velocity is v = −x₀ω sin ωt. What is the phase difference between displacement and velocity in SHM?
samples.why: Since cos ωt and sin ωt are a quarter of a cycle apart, displacement and velocity differ in phase by π/2 (90°). This matches the motion: velocity is maximum when displacement is zero (mean position) and zero when displacement is maximum (extremes).

wrong.0: If they were in phase, velocity would be largest at the extreme positions, but the body is momentarily at rest there.
wrong.2: A phase difference of π would put velocity at zero when displacement is zero, but the speed is maximum at the mean position.
wrong.3: A phase difference of 2π is the same as being in phase, which does not match SHM.

samples.stem: A string under a tension of 64 N has a mass per unit length of 0.01 kg m⁻¹. The speed of transverse waves on it is:
samples.why: The speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string is v = √(F/m). Here F/m = 64 N ÷ 0.01 kg m⁻¹ = 6400 m² s⁻², so v = √6400 = 80 m s⁻¹. A tighter or lighter string carries waves faster.

wrong.0: 8 m s⁻¹ is √64, which leaves out the mass per unit length. F must first be divided by 0.01.
wrong.2: 640 is 64 ÷ 0.1, a slip in the decimal, and the square root is not taken either.
wrong.3: 6400 is F/m, which equals v² in m² s⁻². The square root must be taken.

samples.stem: A spring of constant k is stretched from its mean position to x₀. The average force applied during the stretching, used to find the stored energy, is
samples.why: The force needed to stretch a spring grows steadily, from 0 at x = 0 to kx₀ at x = x₀ (Hooke's law). For a force that rises uniformly, the average is (0 + kx₀)/2 = kx₀/2. The work done, and so the stored energy, is average force × x₀ = ½kx₀².

wrong.0: kx₀ is the final, maximum force at full stretch, not the average over the whole stretch.
wrong.2: 2kx₀ is twice the largest force ever applied, so it cannot be the average.
wrong.3: ½kx₀² is the work done, an energy measured in joules, not a force.

samples.stem: When the angle between force and displacement is more than 90°, the work done by the force is:
samples.why: Work is W = Fd cos θ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement. For angles between 90° and 180°, cos θ is negative, so the work is negative. This means the force acts partly against the motion, as friction does on a sliding block.

wrong.0: Work is positive only when θ is less than 90°, so that the force has a component along the motion.
wrong.1: Work is zero only when θ is exactly 90°, because cos 90° = 0. Above 90°, cos θ is negative.
wrong.2: Work is greatest when θ = 0°, since cos 0° = 1. Beyond 90° the work is negative, not maximum.

samples.stem: A student pushes hard against a fixed wall for one minute. The work done on the wall is:
options: zero, because there is no displacement
large, because a large force is applied
equal to the force times one minute
negative, because the wall pushes back
samples.why: In physics, work is done only when a force moves its point of application: W = Fd cos θ. The wall does not move, so d = 0 and W = 0, however large the force or however long it is applied. The student's muscles get tired from internal effort, but no work is done on the wall.

wrong.1: A large force alone does not give work. Work also needs a displacement, and here the wall's displacement is zero.
wrong.2: Force × time is impulse, not work. Work is force × displacement, and the displacement is zero.
wrong.3: Negative work needs a displacement opposite to the force. The wall does not move at all, so the work is zero, not negative.

samples.stem: A force of 50 N pulls a box 4 m along the floor. The force acts at 60° to the direction of motion. The work done by the force is:
samples.why: When the force makes an angle θ with the displacement, only its component F cos θ along the motion does work, so W = Fd cos θ. Here W = 50 N × 4 m × cos 60° = 200 × 0.5 = 100 J.

wrong.0: 12.5 comes from dividing the force by the distance (50 ÷ 4). Work is force multiplied by displacement, not divided.
wrong.2: 173 J uses sin 60° (0.866) instead of cos 60°. The sine gives the component perpendicular to the motion, which does no work.
wrong.3: 200 J is Fd with no angle factor. It would be correct only if the force acted along the direction of motion.

samples.subject: Biology
samples.stem: What does the abbreviation HIV stand for?
samples.why: HIV stands for Human Immunodeficiency Virus. It infects and destroys helper T lymphocytes, which coordinate the immune response. As their numbers fall, the immune system becomes very weak, and the person develops AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome).

wrong.1: There is no virus with this name. The I in HIV stands for immunodeficiency.
wrong.2: This is not what HIV stands for. The H stands for human and the I for immunodeficiency.
wrong.3: HIV is a virus that causes disease, not a vaccine. The V stands for virus.

samples.subject: Biology
samples.stem: Which description fits the Golgi apparatus?
options: Centre that modifies and packs cell products
samples.why: The Golgi apparatus is a stack of flattened sacs. It receives proteins and lipids from the ER, modifies them, for example by adding carbohydrate, then sorts and packs them into vesicles. These vesicles are sent for secretion or for use inside the cell.

wrong.0: Energy production as ATP is the job of mitochondria, through aerobic respiration.
wrong.2: Genetic material (DNA) is stored in the nucleus, not in the Golgi apparatus.
wrong.3: Proteins are made on ribosomes. The Golgi modifies them afterwards.

samples.subject: Biology
samples.stem: A cell pumps substances against their concentration gradient and needs a steady supply of ATP to do so. Which organelle supplies this energy?
samples.why: Pumping substances against their concentration gradient is active transport, and it uses energy from ATP. Most of a cell's ATP is made by aerobic respiration in the mitochondria. So the mitochondrion supplies the energy for this process.

wrong.0: The nucleus contains DNA and controls the cell's activities, but it does not make ATP.
wrong.2: The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages proteins and lipids. It does not produce ATP.
wrong.3: The endoplasmic reticulum makes and transports proteins and lipids. It is not the main source of ATP.

samples.subject: Biology
samples.stem: A surgeon repairs the heart valve that stops blood flowing back into the right ventricle. Which valve is it?
samples.why: Blood leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary artery to go to the lungs. At the base of the pulmonary artery is the pulmonary semilunar valve. When the ventricle relaxes, this valve closes and stops blood flowing back into the right ventricle.

wrong.0: The mitral (bicuspid) valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle, on the other side of the heart.
wrong.1: The aortic semilunar valve stops blood flowing back from the aorta into the left ventricle.
wrong.2: The tricuspid valve stops blood flowing back from the right ventricle into the right atrium, not into the ventricle.

samples.subject: Chemistry
samples.stem: What mainly holds the atoms of a noble gas together in the liquid or solid state?
samples.why: Noble gas atoms have full outer shells, so they form no bonds and are non-polar. The only attraction between them is the London dispersion force. It arises when a moving electron cloud creates a temporary dipole, which induces a dipole in a neighbouring atom.

wrong.0: Noble gases have full outer shells, so they do not share electrons to form covalent bonds.
wrong.1: Noble gas atoms do not lose or gain electrons, so there are no ions to attract each other.
wrong.2: Hydrogen bonds need H attached to N, O or F. Noble gas atoms contain no hydrogen.

samples.subject: Chemistry
samples.stem: Which test distinguishes methyl ketones from other ketones?
samples.why: Methyl ketones contain the CH₃CO– group. Warming with iodine and NaOH turns this group into a yellow precipitate of iodoform (CHI₃). Ketones without a CH₃ next to the C=O give no precipitate, so the iodoform test separates the two.

wrong.0: Tollens' test (silver mirror) distinguishes aldehydes from ketones. No ketone gives a silver mirror.
wrong.1: Silver nitrate is used to test for halide ions, not to tell ketones apart.
wrong.3: The Lucas test uses ZnCl₂ and HCl to classify alcohols as primary, secondary or tertiary.

samples.subject: Physics
samples.stem: The distance a wave travels in one second is its
samples.why: Wave speed is the distance a wave travels per unit time, so in one second it covers a distance equal to its speed. It is linked to frequency and wavelength by v = fλ: in one second f waves pass, each λ long.

wrong.0: Wavelength is the distance between two neighbouring crests (or troughs), not the distance travelled in a second.
wrong.1: Amplitude is the greatest displacement of a particle from its mean position.
wrong.2: Displacement is how far a particle is from its mean position at a given instant.

samples.subject: Physics
samples.stem: In which process is work done by the gas entirely at the expense of its internal energy?
samples.why: In an adiabatic process no heat enters or leaves the gas, so Q = 0. The first law Q = ΔU + W then gives W = −ΔU. All the work done by the gas comes from its own internal energy, so the gas cools as it expands.

wrong.0: In an isochoric (constant-volume) process the gas does no work at all, since its volume does not change.
wrong.1: In an isobaric process heat is supplied, so the work comes partly from that heat, not only from internal energy.
wrong.2: In an isothermal process ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, so the work comes entirely from heat taken in.

samples.subject: English
samples.stem: Choose the word that fills the blank: The director ______ film was a blockbuster earned a lot of money.
samples.why: Whose is the possessive relative pronoun: it links a noun to its owner. Here the film belongs to the director, so "the director whose film was a blockbuster" is correct. The whole clause "whose film was a blockbuster" tells us which director earned a lot of money.

wrong.0: Who's is a short form of "who is" or "who has". "The director who is film was a blockbuster" makes no sense.
wrong.1: Whom is the object form of who, as in "the director whom we met". It cannot show possession, and it cannot be followed directly by "film".
wrong.3: Which is used for things and animals, not people, and it does not show ownership. "The director which film" is wrong on both counts.

samples.subject: Logical Reasoning
samples.stem: A belief can be called true and reasonable when it is
samples.why: In critical thinking a belief is reasonable when it is supported by evidence and sound logic. Evidence is something that can be checked, such as observations or test results, and logic links that evidence to the claim. A belief built this way is the one most likely to be true.

wrong.0: Popularity is not evidence. Many people once believed the Sun moved around the Earth, and they were wrong.
wrong.1: Feelings tell us what we want to be true, not what is true. A belief can feel right and still be false.
wrong.3: The age of a source does not make it correct. Old books can contain errors that later evidence has corrected.
